He, glory be to Him, does not teach us history; rather, He places before us the lesson and the snapshot He wants within this context. For this reason, He, glory be to Him, does not speak in this surah about the birth of Musa (Moses) and how He inspired his mother to cast him into the river, nor does the incident of his going to Madyan (Midian) and his meeting with our master Shu'ayb (Jethro) appear. Instead, here He speaks, glory be to Him, about the mission of our master Musa with Fir'awn (Pharaoh). He says, glory be to Him:

﴿And Musa said: "O Pharaoh, indeed I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds."﴾ (7:104)

The Qur'an explains the matter of Musa's proclamation to Pharaoh and his people, namely that God is One and Unique, and He is the Lord of the worlds. The people of Pharaoh believed in the existence of one god for the heaven and another for the earth, so Musa conveys to them that God is one:

﴿He said: "Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, if you are certain."﴾ (26:24) (Surat al-Shu'ara')

We find Musa enumerating the word of lordship (rububiyyah) in other verses, in order to bring forth the aspect in which the deceit of Pharaoh's lordship was inserted. They believed that the heaven had a god and the earth had another god, so Musa said: I am speaking of the One God who is the Lord of the heaven and the earth together; there is no god but God alone. And they believed that the East had a god and the West had a god, so Musa informed them that He is one God. And they believed that the living had a god and lord, and the dead had a god and lord, so Musa said to them:

﴿"Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the earliest ones."﴾ (26:26) (Surat al-Shu'ara')

And here Musa conveys to Pharaoh and his people:

﴿"Indeed I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds."﴾ (part of 7:104)

Since Moses is a messenger from the Lord of the worlds, he says nothing but the truth.

Therefore, the truth continues on the tongue of Moses: ﴿It is fitting for me that I should not say about Allah except the truth. I have come to you with a clear proof from your Lord, so send with me the Children of Israel (105).﴾

Which of these matters is the one that needs a proof: the claim that he is a messenger from the Lord of the worlds? This statement shows us that Moses differed with Pharaoh first on three points: that Moses is a messenger, that the worlds have one Lord, and that he speaks only the truth. These, then, are three points of dispute between Moses and Pharaoh. But Pharaoh disagreed with Moses on only one matter, namely: is he a messenger conveying from Allah the true word? So what did Pharaoh ask of him? He asked for proof that he is a messenger from the Lord of the worlds. This makes clear that Pharaoh knew that the world has a higher Lord.

Likewise, Pharaoh did not stand against Moses on the question that the worlds have a Lord, and that this Lord cannot be understood by every person in what He intends, so a messenger must be sent. Rather, Pharaoh stood against him only on the question: is Moses a messenger conveying from Allah or not? That is why Moses says:

﴿It is fitting for me that I should not say about Allah except the truth. I have come to you with a clear proof from your Lord, so send with me the Children of Israel (105)﴾ (Surat al-A'raf). It is as if Moses's mission before Pharaoh was to free the Children of Israel. We know that the story of the Children of Israel began in the days of the Prophet Ya'qub and his son Yusuf, when the brothers plotted against their brother Yusuf and deliberated about killing him, or casting him away on some land, or throwing him into the depths of the well. The Truth has brought the story of the Children of Israel in stages, so that we may proceed step by step with the emotion of it. The stages of psychological emotion before one you hate take two forms: a form that indicates the escalation of mercy in your heart, and a form that indicates the escalation of evil in your heart. For example: suppose you have an adversary who devised a plot against you, and you tell your brothers what this adversary did and how you want to avenge yourself, saying: "I want to avenge myself by slapping him twice." Then you escalate the evil, saying: "I want to kill him with a bullet." This is the way of the wicked. But the good person says: "I do not want to kill him, slap him, insult him, or revile him," and this is an escalation in goodness. So, the escalation of revenge or forgiveness differs according to the strength of good or evil in the soul. Thus we find the brothers of Yusuf, as they plotted against him, saying: ﴿Joseph and his brother are dearer to our father than we are, though we are a band (8)﴾ (Surat Yusuf, verse 8). They acknowledge that they are a strong group, and they envy Yusuf and his brother for the father's love for them, and they object to that, and they show the proof that Yusuf and his brother are dearer to the father than they are. The Qur'an mentions this proof so that we know its importance and that no one overlooks it. The heart of the Prophet Ya'qub was with Yusuf and his brother because of their youth and weakness, while his other sons were grown, strong and mighty, because Allah, glory be to Him, placed in the hearts of fathers and mothers mercy in proportion to the weakness of the young child. The small child is the one who needs care and attention, and the heart of the mother and father is with the sick or absent son. That is why, when a wise woman was asked: "Which of your children do you love most?" she said: "The small one until he grows up, the absent one until he returns, and the sick one until he recovers."

So the saying of Yusuf's brothers, ﴿and we are a band﴾, is evidence against them. Logic required that they realize that, since they are a band, their father's heart must be with Yusuf and his brother, for both were young and in need of care. By the nature of the sons of Ya'qub as tribes and descendants of prophets, we find them escalating toward good rather than evil. They began by declaring a desire to kill him, then replaced that with casting him onto a land far away and remote so that they might be rid of him and clear the face of their father for themselves, then replaced that with throwing him into the depths of the well. They began with killing in a moment of fierce anger, then they relented from killing to casting him on the ground, that is, leaving him in a place where he would be exposed to getting lost, then they relented from that too and settled for throwing him into the bottom of the well, where some caravan might pick him up. Did they want to harm him, or were they thinking of his rescue? So this is an escalation toward good.

Events followed with Sayyidna Yusuf, and the Children of Israel settled with him in Egypt and grew in number. When we survey history, we find that when the Truth, glory be to Him, spoke of the kings of Egypt, He singled out some of them by the title Pharaoh and some by the title king; so there is a Pharaoh and there is a king. If you look at the ancient period, the Truth says: ﴿and Pharaoh of the stakes (10)﴾ (Surat al-Fajr).

Thus we find the Truth calling the ruler of Egypt "Pharaoh," and in the days of Sayyidna Musa too He calls him Pharaoh. But in the days of Yusuf, peace be upon him, He did not call him Pharaoh, rather He called him king:

﴿And the king said: Bring him to me (50)﴾ (Surat Yusuf).

After the French scholar Champollion discovered the Rosetta Stone, we learned that the period in which Sayyidna Yusuf entered Egypt was not one in which the Pharaohs ruled Egypt; rather, the rulers were the Hyksos shepherd kings. The Qur'an has concealed this historical fact when it named the rulers of Egypt before Yusuf "Pharaohs," while in the period when Sayyidna Yusuf came it called them "the kings." These are the ones who raided Egypt, ruled it, and were aided and served by the Children of Israel, who looked after their interests. After the Egyptians expelled the Hyksos, the Pharaohs turned their evil against those who had aided the Hyksos, and so they began to subjugate the Children of Israel for having helped the Hyksos during their rule over Egypt. Allah willed to rescue them through Moses, peace be upon him, and therefore the Truth says on the tongue of Moses: ﴿And Moses said: O Pharaoh, I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds (104). It is fitting for me that I should not say about Allah except the truth. I have come to you with a clear proof from your Lord, so send with me the Children of Israel (105)﴾ (Surat al-A'raf). It is as if Moses wants to free the Children of Israel; as for the matter of divinity and the lordship of Pharaoh, it came incidentally.

Pharaoh said: ﴿If you have come with a sign, then produce it, if you are among the truthful.﴾

Thus Pharaoh confronts Moses, asking him to show the sign if he is one of the truthful. So Pharaoh believes that God has signs which establish the truthfulness of the Messenger, as evidenced by his saying to him: "Bring it, if you are among the truthful."

Al-Sha'rawi on Surah 7, verse 107:

Moses, peace be upon him, reveals (the matter)... The verse: ﴿So he cast down his staff, and behold, it was a manifest serpent.﴾

﴿So he cast down his staff, and behold, it was a manifest serpent.﴾:

This casting had a previous experience of another kind, when he went out with his family from Madyan and saw a fire, and after that he said to his family: ﴿Stay here; indeed, I have perceived a fire﴾ (part of verse 10, Surah Ta-Ha). Then he heard an address: ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Moses? He said, "It is my staff; I lean upon it and I beat down (leaves) with it for my sheep, and I have in it other uses."﴾ (Surah Ta-Ha). When he was asked, ﴿What is that in your right hand, O Moses?﴾, it would have sufficed for him to answer, "My staff," and there was no need to say, "It is," nor to explain and say that he leans on it and that he has other uses in it; for the Truth did not ask him what he does with his staff. So Moses' answer exceeded the required measure in the address, and some think that it was obligatory to give an answer in proportion to the question. But whoever says that forgets that no one renounces delight in addressing God. When Moses, peace be upon him, said: ﴿It is my staff; I lean upon it and I beat down (leaves) with it for my sheep﴾ (part of verse 18, Surah Ta-Ha), Moses felt and corrected himself for the dignity of the One addressed, and his eagerness in the address was out of love for intimacy with God. Yet he felt that he was close to going beyond (the bounds), so he said: ﴿And I have in it other uses,﴾ (that is, he could have said, "many uses for the staff"). So the staff had more than one casting: the casting of training and practice, in preparation for meeting Pharaoh, when the Truth commanded him: ﴿He said, "Cast it down, O Moses." So he cast it down, and behold, it was a serpent, moving swiftly﴾ (Surah Ta-Ha). Then what happened? God said to him: ﴿He said, "Take it and fear not; We will return it to its first state."﴾ (Surah Ta-Ha). At the moment he feared, this showed that what happened to the staff was not of the kind of magic; for the magician, when he casts his staff or rope, sees it as a staff or rope, while others see it as a serpent. That is why the Truth says of the magicians: ﴿They bewitched the eyes of the people﴾ (part of verse 116, Surah al-A'raf). This shows that the reality of a thing in magic remains as it is in the eyes of the magician. But Moses "sensed fear within himself," which shows that the staff had passed from its wooden nature and become a serpent.

It was possible that the staff would sprout leaves and turn green, although it had been a dry branch. Had that happened, it would also have been a miracle, but God transferred it in two transfers: He moved it from inanimate matter and carried it past the stage of plant life to the stage of animal life.

It is as though the Truth, All-Knowing from eternity, responds to those who want to stir confusion about the casting of the staff, since some ignorant people thought that this is repetition in the telling of one story. They did not notice that the aspect of the casting of the staff was distinct. In the Qur'an there are three castings of the staff: the casting of training, when God chose Moses as a messenger and informed him of that at the Sinai valley: ﴿Indeed, I am God; there is no deity except Me, so worship Me﴾ (part of verse 14, Surah Ta-Ha); and after that He said to him: ﴿What is that in your right hand, O Moses? He said, "It is my staff"﴾ (Surah Ta-Ha). The casting of training for the task had the aim of reassuring Moses, so that when he undertook it before Pharaoh he would undertake it certain that the staff would respond to him and turn into a serpent at the mere casting. Had God merely told him in news, "When you go to Pharaoh, cast the staff and it will turn into a serpent," his heart might not have been content with this matter. So God willed to train him on it practically, so that he would know that the staff would respond to him when he cast it, becoming a serpent. That was its first casting. The second casting was at the time when Pharaoh came to be informed of his mission, that he is a messenger of the Lord of the worlds, and to be informed of the clear sign; and this is what we are now concerned with in this verse, about which we speak with our faith-inspired reflections.

Then there is a third casting, which is the casting of challenge to the magicians. Because each casting has its place, do not ever say that this is repetition. Rather, it is establishing multiple situations and circumstances: each situation requires what it demands, and one snapshot here does not suffice in place of another snapshot there. ﴿So he cast down his staff, and behold, it was a manifest serpent.﴾ (Surah al-A'raf).

At one point He says of the staff: ﴿As if it were a jann.﴾ And the skeptics among the Orientalists, who doubt the words of God, say: how can He say at one time that it was a manifest serpent, then at another time say: ﴿and behold, it was a moving snake﴾, and a third time say: ﴿as if it were a jann﴾? We say: there is a difference between things that contradict one another and things that complement one another. It was a serpent at one time, a snake at a second, and a jann; for the serpent is the long, light-moving one, the snake is the frightening mass when coiled, and the jann is the snake of horrifying form. So it appeared each time in an image that terrifies whoever sees it, and each time it had a form: at one time a serpent, at another a snake, and a third time a jann, or it is a serpent to one who is frightened by serpents, a snake to one frightened by snakes, and a jann to one frightened by jann. That is why you find that spreading ambiguity is itself clarification of the ambiguous thing.

An example of that is the Truth's making the matter of death ambiguous: it is not governed by age, nor by a cause, nor by a time. In this there is ambiguity about its time and ambiguity about its cause, which makes it a widespread clarification that one meets by any cause, at any time or in any place. Thus the ambiguity comes here so as to give us complete images. Some Orientalists said: Muslims receive the Qur'an with awe and amazement, and do not move their minds to see the contradictions in it; but a non-Muslim who reads the Qur'an finds in it many different things. They said verbatim: "You know, in matters of language, that a simile comes only to attach an unknown to a known," so one says: "You know so-and-so," and you say: "No, by God, I do not know him." He says to you: "He is like so-and-so, in height, in breadth, in form"; so he has attached an unknown to a known in order to clarify it. How then does the Qur'an attach an unknown to an unknown? This does not give an image, as when the Qur'an spoke of the tree of Zaqqum: ﴿It is a tree that springs from the root of Hellfire. Its shoots are like the heads of devils﴾ (Surah al-Saffat). How can a tree exist in Hellfire? These are contradictory things, for a tree has greenness and needs irrigation and moisture, while Hellfire is fire and dryness. Moreover, the devil's form is unknown to humans, and the tree of Zaqqum is unknown because it will come in the Hereafter; so how does God liken an unknown to an unknown? The Orientalists used this as evidence that Muslims take the Qur'an with amazement and do not investigate it. We answer them: you do not know the Arabic language as a native faculty; you have learned it as a craft, and you have not grasped the truth that the Qur'an came in the language of the Arabs. The Arabs have imagined things in which they saw ugliness and repulsiveness, as when they said: "and sharpened, blue, like the fangs of ghouls," though the ghoul is a being that does not exist; yet they imagined the frightening ghoul and that it has fangs... etc.

So the simile may be for something imagined in people's minds. The essence of simile is to attach an unknown so that it may be known; we do not know the tree of Zaqqum, and we have not seen the heads of devils; thus God attached an unknown to an unknown. And why did He not bring it in a known form? Because He, glory be to Him, wants to spread clarification, generalize the benefit, and multiply it; for fear requires something frightening, and what frightens differs according to those who see it: something may frighten you but not frighten another, and you may find something ugly that another does not find ugly. That is why we gave an example earlier. We said: if we brought together a group of the greatest cartoonists in the world and said to them, "Draw us an image of the devil; imagine the devil and draw him," would they agree on one form of him? No, because each artist will draw the devil from the inspiration of what frightens him.

God said, in the image of the tree of Zaqqum: ﴿its shoots are like the heads of devils,﴾ so that every hearer imagines from the devil's image what frightens him, and the benefit becomes general in warning against that tree. Had He stated it in one single image, it would have frightened one people and not frightened others.

Similarly is the matter of Moses' staff: it is at one time a serpent, at another a jann, at another a snake, and all are images of one frightening thing. Here in Surah al-A'raf the Truth says: ﴿So he cast down his staff, and behold, it was a manifest serpent.﴾

His saying ﴿and behold﴾ shows the suddenness that stunned Pharaoh: the staff turned into a huge serpent in the twinkling of an eye, by the mere casting. Among the benefits of training Moses, peace be upon him, on casting the staff in the Sinai valley is that Moses would not be seized by surprise when he casts it before Pharaoh; rather, surprise would seize Pharaoh. The training was first to convince Moses and guarantee that he would not fear at the moment of execution. Moses did fear it during the training, because the staff became a real serpent and a snake. Had it been of the kind of magic, it would have remained a staff in the eye of the magician, and he would not have feared it. So his fear of it at the time of the training is evidence that it truly transformed, not imagined; and that is the difference between a miracle and magic: the miracle is reality, and magic is imagination. This is what will make the magicians fall down prostrate, because they were stunned by what happened.

﴿So he cast down his staff, and behold, it was a manifest serpent.﴾ (Surah al-A'raf).

"Manifest" means clear, its frightening features evident to none can hide.

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary on Surah al-A'raf, verse 108:

Then Musa (peace be upon him) presents the second sign, and the Truth (al-Haqq) says: ﴿And he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white to the onlookers.﴾

This is another miracle. His saying "and drew out" (wa-naza'a) means taking the hand out with difficulty, as if something were resisting the withdrawal of the hand. For if the withdrawal of the hand were easy, the Truth would not have said "and drew out his hand," because naz' (drawing out) indicates that something resists. An example is the saying of the Truth: ﴿Say: O Allah, Owner of Sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will and You strip sovereignty from whom You will﴾ (part of verse 26, Surah Ali 'Imran). Stripping away sovereignty is not an easy matter, for usually the possessor of sovereignty clings to his dominion, yet the Truth strips it from him. Likewise His saying "and drew out his hand": this indicates that his hand had a placement, and drawing it out forcefully had another placement, as if it had been in a place it was eager to keep. So there is one snapshot that shows the insertion and another that shows the drawing out, and these are two operations.

He, glorified is He, said in a second verse: ﴿And insert your hand into your bosom; it will come out white, without harm﴾ (part of verse 12, Surah al-Naml). The "bosom" (jayb) is the place through which the head enters the garment. Although in our days we call "jayb" any thing we make a receptacle for what we love, the original idea was that when a person wants to keep something, he places it in front of him and under his hand; then people made pockets (juyub) in garments, and they were named juyub for this reason.

And the Truth said in another place:

﴿And press your hand to your side; it will come out white, without harm﴾ (part of verse 22, Surah Ta-Ha). So there is insertion and withdrawal. Each verse came with one of the snapshots: one verse clarified the entry of the hand into the bosom, another clarified pressing the hand to the side (janah), and a third clarified the drawing out of the hand. These are multiple snapshots which together form the complete picture, so that we understand that the stories in the Qur'an are not repetitive; repetition may occur in the phrase, but every repetition has a foundational snapshot, and when we survey them we perceive the complete pillars of the story. All these snapshots gather for us the story. We said earlier that the conflict between Pharaoh and Musa arises only from enmity, and for the conflict to flare up, the enmity must be mutual. If one were an enemy while the other felt no hostility, there would be no fierce contention; he might overlook his opponent, take the dispute lightly, forgive him, and the matter would subside. But what makes enmity blaze, intensify, and its flame rise is that it be reciprocal. The Qur'an presents one snapshot establishing Pharaoh's enmity toward Musa, and another establishing Musa's enmity toward Pharaoh. The Truth says: ﴿He shall take him, an enemy to Me and an enemy to him﴾ (part of verse 39, Surah Ta-Ha): this establishes Pharaoh's enmity toward Musa. And the Truth says: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become to them an enemy and a grief﴾ (part of verse 8, Surah al-Qasas): this establishes that Musa was an enemy to them. Both snapshots complete each other to give us the complete picture.

And the Truth says here: ﴿And he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white to the onlookers﴾ (Surah al-A'raf). We know that Musa was dark-complexioned, so the whiteness in his hand would contrast with the rest of his skin colour, and his hand became white such that, at the moment people see it, its light would catch their attention and draw their eyes. It was not the whiteness that comes with darkness resulting from leprosy (baras); no, because the Truth says in another verse: ﴿It will come out white, without harm﴾ (part of verse 22, Surah Ta-Ha).

As you see, each snapshot comes to confirm and complete the picture. So His saying "white to the onlookers" indicates that its light was radiant and bright, drawing the attention of all people to it, and this would only be the case if it had lustre, sheen, and brilliance. And His saying "white, without harm" affirms that this whiteness is not a disease.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 7, verse 109:

God, glory be to Him, continues: ﴿The chiefs of Pharaoh's people said: "Indeed, this is a skilled sorcerer."﴾

We have learned that al-mala' (the chiefs, the notables) are the people who occupy the councils and fill them, or who fill the eyes with awe and the hearts with reverence. Here they are those close to Pharaoh. It is as if they possessed an idea and knowledge about magic. In Surat ash-Shu'ara' the true word came: ﴿He said to the chiefs around him: "Indeed, this is a skilled sorcerer."﴾ (Surat ash-Shu'ara', 34). So this is a report that the statement came from the chiefs, while the other verse has the statement on the tongue of Pharaoh. There is no slightest contradiction in this. It is permissible that Pharaoh said he is a sorcerer, and also that the chiefs said he is a sorcerer. Thoughts coincide regarding a known matter agreed upon. Something similar happened in the Qur'an when verses were revealed about the creation of man and his development, that he was a clot, then a lump of flesh, etc., and the scribe of the revelation said aloud: ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾ (part of verse 14, Surat al-Mu'minun). From Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "My Lord agreed with me in four things: this verse was revealed: ﴿And We created man from an extract of clay﴾ to the end of the verse, and I said: ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators,﴾ and then it was revealed: ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators.﴾"(1) And from Zayd ibn Thabit al-Ansari, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) dictated to me this verse: ﴿And We created man from an extract of clay﴾ to His saying: ﴿...another creation﴾, and Mu'adh said: ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators,﴾ and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) laughed. Mu'adh said to him: "What are you laughing at, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "With it you have been concluded: ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators.﴾"(2)

The thoughts came in a state stirred by the feelings of faith at the moment of the revelation, with the stages of human creation.

What prevents thoughts from coinciding, so that the thought arises with Pharaoh and with the chiefs, and they say it? Or Pharaoh may have said it, and, as is the custom of followers and underlings, when their master says something they repeat it.

﴿The chiefs of Pharaoh's people said: "Indeed, this is a skilled sorcerer."﴾ (Surat al-A'raf). They did not describe the deed of our master Musa merely as sorcery, but exaggerated in it and said: "Indeed, he is a skilled sorcerer." They added what came on their tongues in the Qur'an in this surah.

1. Narrated by Ibn Abi Hatim.
2. Narrated by Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Kathir cited it in his tafsir and said: "Its chain contains Jabir ibn Zayd al-Ju'fi, who is very weak, and we consider the report of our master 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, to be more sound."

It is a calamity that came upon Pharaoh, who claimed divinity, and a calamity upon those around him who agreed with him. So how would he confront it, so that he might remain in his bearing and his dignity? He said of Musa: "Indeed he is a sorcerer," in order to turn the people who had seen Musa's miracles away from faith in him and from being convinced of him, and [in order to turn them away from the belief] that he is the Messenger of the Lord of the worlds. After that, Pharaoh stirred up their nationalism, excited and roused their zeal, and moved their attachment to their homeland, so he said: ﴿He wants to drive you out of your land, so what do you advise?﴾ (7:110).

They accused Musa, peace be upon him, of wanting to drive the people out of their land by their sorcery. This statement from Pharaoh and those with him has a purpose, which is to agitate and incite the people, because Pharaoh had convinced the people that he was a god. And now his divinity was nearly collapsing in an instant, so he said of Musa that he is a sorcerer, among a people accustomed to sorcery. His words ﴿so what do you advise?﴾, spoken on the tongue of the chiefs (al-mala') of Pharaoh's people, indicate that the speaker of the phrase is lower than those he addresses. It was supposed that Pharaoh was the one with authority over everyone, and the statement ﴿so what do you advise?﴾ indicates that the one who gives orders in matters like this is Pharaoh. This suggests that Pharaoh had realized that his standing had fallen and that he had come down from his arrogance and haughtiness. Or it may be that this came from Pharaoh as a way of comforting the hearts of those around him, and that he would not decide any matter without consultation (mashwara). So how do you consult people, O Pharaoh, when you have implanted in people that you are a god? Does a god consult a mortal? Your words here carry your own failure, because you claim divinity and then want to seek help from the command of one who is created.

Al-Sha'rawi, Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66), on surah 7, verse 111:

The Truthful (Exalted is He) says:

﴿They said: "Put him off, and his brother, and send into the cities gatherers,"﴾.

And "arjih" means: delay him, like His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿And others are deferred (murjawn)﴾ (Qur'an 9:106), meaning: they are deferred in respect of the judgment upon them, namely the three who stayed behind from the expedition and were left behind, and their matter was deferred until His saying (Exalted is He) was revealed concerning them: ﴿And upon the three who were left behind﴾ (Qur'an 9:118), etc. As for their saying: ﴿Put him off, and his brother﴾ (Qur'an 7:111): this is how the request for deferment was made, because the matter is too grave to be handled hastily; rather, it needs the decision on it to be postponed until the chieftains gather and everyone sees how to confront it. It is not a trivial matter, because in it is the overturning of Pharaoh's divinity, and in this is the demolition of Pharaoh's authority and the ending of the benefit they themselves derive from that authority. So when he had said to them: ﴿What do you advise?﴾ (Qur'an 7:110).

It was as if he were asking them for an opinion immediately, but they said that the matter needs deliberation and slowness, and the first degrees of slowness and deliberation are that the people who understand magic be summoned. So, as long as we are saying about Moses that he is a sorcerer, let us confront him with what we have of magic. Pharaoh's acceptance of this counsel is the demolition of his divinity, because he claims to be a god and seeks help from one who is a god to them, namely the sorcerers, and the sorcerers are his followers.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 7, verse 112:

His words, the Truth, on their tongues: ﴿And send into the cities gatherers﴾ (part of verse 111, surah al-A'raf) indicate that magic was widespread and scattered throughout the cities. God, glorified is He, followed this statement on the tongue of the chiefs with His words:

﴿They will bring you every skilled sorcerer﴾.

As for the orientalists, who want to cast doubt upon us regarding the Qur'an, they said: "Why did it say in surah al-Shu'ara': ﴿every skilled sorcerer﴾?" It is as if these orientalists want to distinguish between ﴿sahir 'alim﴾ (knowing sorcerer) and ﴿sahhar 'alim﴾ (knowing sorcerer, in intensive form). Because they do not know the language, they did not notice that "sahhar" conveys intensification in two respects. The word "sahir" means that he practises magic, while "sahhar" means that he is thorough in mastering magic. Intensive forms always come either to denote the greatness of the event or to denote its repetition. So "sahhar" means that his magic is very powerful, or that he works magic in every situation: in terms of repetition, he is capable of magic, and in terms of magnitude, he is also capable. And since those who speak are many, one says "sahir," another says "sahhar," and so on. The Qur'an covers every scene.

﴿They said: "Delay him and his brother, and send into the cities gatherers, who will bring you every skilled sorcerer."﴾ (surah al-A'raf, 111–112)

"Gatherers" (hasharin) means those who gather the sorcerers for you and assemble them, not by their own will, but by the power of Pharaoh and the might of his soldiers.

And the Almighty says: ﴿And the magicians came to Pharaoh; they said: "Surely there will be a reward for us if we are the victors."﴾

His words ﴿And the magicians came to Pharaoh﴾ indicate the ruler's might and power, meaning that the moment he uttered the word, the soldiers hastened quickly to gather the magicians. Some Orientalists have also indulged in this scene, asking: "And why did he come with a different statement in another surah, when he said: ﴿Is there indeed for us a reward?﴾ (part of verse 41, Surat al-Shu'ara')?"

He brought it with the interrogative particle hamza (ʾa, the interrogative "is it that…?") there, while in Surat al-A'raf he brought it without the interrogative hamza, and this is a Qur'anic verse. Those who hold this view overlook that every magician among Pharaoh's magicians was moved by an emotion that led him to his aim. The one who asked Pharaoh said: "A-inna" (with the interrogative hamza), whereas the brave one said to Pharaoh: ﴿Surely there is indeed a reward for us﴾. In the interrogative formulation the reward is not certain, since it is possible that Pharaoh would reply that there is no reward for you; but in the declarative formulation ﴿Surely there is indeed a reward for us﴾, meaning that some of the magicians had judged that the existence of a reward was necessary, and the Qur'an has encompassed both this interrogation and this declaration.

Pharaoh's reply to the sorcerers' request for a reward comes next: ﴿He said: "Yes, and indeed you will be among those brought near."﴾

"Na'am" (نعم, "yes") is a particle of answer standing in place of a full sentence, namely: "You shall have a reward." He added also: ﴿and indeed you will be among those brought near.﴾

This is evidence that he was flattering them, or exaggerating in his courtesy toward them, because he was in dire need of them. Thus we find that Pharaoh's divinity has crumbled before the sorcerers, whom he himself claimed as subjects of his godhood.

His saying ﴿among those brought near﴾ indicates the corruption of rule: since he is a ruler, all those ruled ought to be equal in relation to him. But when there are "those brought near," the first circle of them plunders according to its nearness, the second circle plunders likewise, and so too the third and fourth. Thus every circle practices its corruption, so long as people are classified in the sight of the ruler.

For this reason, when the Companions sat listening to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he would treat all the people equally in his regard, so that every person thought he was the closest to the Messenger of Allah's gaze, and he would not bring near or draw close to his gathering anyone except one whom everyone testified was close.

The Exalted says next: ﴿They said, "O Moses, either you throw first or we will be the ones who throw."﴾

We notice that they did not emphasize to Moses their desire that he should throw his staff first. Rather, they emphasized their desire to be the first to throw. So they used the separating pronoun (damir al-fasl), which is "nahnu" ("we"), a word that serves to add emphasis.

We know that whoever comes after another, and whose action follows that of the one before him, is the one upon whose act the judgment will be based, and he must be strong in argument. They wanted to be the ones who come after, while Moses was the one who would begin. But their pride compelled them to begin first. Therefore they used the expression that carries both meanings: ﴿either you throw, or we will be the ones who throw﴾ (part of verse 115, Surat al-A'raf).

So Moses understood that they were eager to begin the throwing themselves, and they used the word "we." Moses thought that it was in his interest that they throw first, because his staff would overtake and swallow what they threw. Therefore comes His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿He said, "Throw." And when they threw, they bewitched the eyes of the people, terrified them, and produced a great magic.﴾ (verse 116)

They therefore bewitched the eyes of the people. Magic, as we know, is a subtle trick that produces a marvel resembling a miracle, as though it breaks the natural law. It differs from the trick performed by the jugglers (al-hawa, sleight-of-hand performers), because the jugglers work through quickness of movement and dexterity of hand to make the matter appear to the people. But "magic" is something else. We know that Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, created every kind according to a law: He created mankind according to a law, He created the jinn according to a law, and He created the angels according to their own law. ﴿And none knows the hosts of your Lord except Him﴾ (Qur'an 74:31).

Every law has its own characteristics and attributes, which suit the element from which it was formed. Man, for example, because he was created from clay, has a density that prevents him from passing through a wall. If you were sitting with an apple behind the wall beside which you sit, its scent and taste would not reach your mouth, because the wall stands between you and that. But if there were a live coal beside the wall on which you lean, its effect could reach you, because fire consists of radiations that pass through things. And since the jinn were created from fire, they possess this property.

﴿Indeed, he and his tribe see you from where you cannot see them﴾ (Qur'an 7:27). If the jinn have a law and mankind has a law, then does the law dominate? No. Rather, the Lord of the law dominates, because He, majestic and exalted, is above the law. Allah therefore teaches a man some of the secrets of His creation, so that he may subjugate the jinn to his service, despite the jinn's quickness of movement. Glory be to Him, He makes clear: do not suppose, O jinn, that you have received your distinctive nature from the element that composes you, for there is the Supreme Power, who has subjected you and others, as is shown by the fact that man, who is of a different element, controls you after Allah has taught him some of the secrets of His creation.

We must always bear in mind that knowledge of the secrets of subjugating the jinn is one of the trials Allah imposes on creation, for He, glory be to Him and exalted, says: ﴿And they teach no one until they say, "We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve"﴾ (Qur'an 2:102). So when Harut and Marut teach a person how to practise magic, they advise the one who wishes to learn magic first, and make clear to him that they are a trial, a test, and say to him: ﴿so do not disbelieve﴾. This shows that whoever learns magic, if he tells you, "I will use it only for good," he is lying, because he says this in a moment of calm toward the creatures. But what if a person catches him unawares, from some direction, and overcomes him in part of his affair while he possesses some of the secrets of magic? Can he control himself? He said he was trustworthy at the time of receiving the knowledge, but will he remain trustworthy at the time of using it? Whoever learns magic may use it to take revenge on others, and thereby the equality of opportunity is lost. We know that equality of opportunity is what protects people, gives some of them security from others, and holds each person to his limit. If a person takes a weapon that others do not have, he may use it against someone who does not possess its like. A human who takes the weapon of using the jinn is taking a weapon that his fellow human does not possess, and so he has taken an opportunity stronger than others', and in this there is a trial, because a person may succeed in it or fail, and so not obtain what he seeks. His words, glory be to Him, ﴿so do not disbelieve﴾, indicate that they knew the natures of human beings: that when they take a higher opportunity, they may be guaranteed in the moment of the calm of their souls, but they are not guaranteed on the day their souls are troubled.

﴿So they learn from them that by which they separate a man from his wife, and they cannot harm anyone thereby except by the permission of Allah﴾ (Qur'an 2:102).

Since the Truth is the One who gave them this power, He, glory be to Him, is able to take it from them, just as Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, grants a person the power to be wealthy and able to buy a firearm and train in shooting. This man, in the hour of his anger, may imagine that he can settle his dispute with another, or end his anger with any other person, by firing bullets at him. But if he did not have a "pistol," his anger might end with a kind word he hears. So when Allah prevents something, He wishes to show mercy. Therefore He says: ﴿And they teach no one until they say, "We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve."﴾

In this there is a warning to whoever learns such a matter, and Allah wishes to protect His creation from this affair. It is enough for us to know that He, glory be to Him, has said: ﴿And they cannot harm anyone thereby except by the permission of Allah﴾.

If you were to follow these people, they would subjugate you and drain you, and Allah would leave you to them because you believed in them. But if you say, "O Allah, You have empowered some of Your creation with magic and evil, but You have reserved for Yourself the permission for harm, so I seek refuge in what You have reserved from what You have empowered them over, by the truth of Your saying: ﴿And they cannot harm anyone thereby except by the permission of Allah﴾," then Allah will not enable them over you. But if you respond and go along with them, they will drain you. Allah wished to expose this kind of operation, and so He said, on the tongues of the magicians whom Pharaoh summoned: ﴿Indeed, for us there will surely be a reward?﴾ (Qur'an 26:41). It is as though they admit the deficiency in themselves: despite their claim to the power to perform miracles, they are unable to earn enough to meet their needs, and therefore they asked Pharaoh for a reward. This is the condition of those who work in magic and charlatanry: they claim power while suffering poverty and want. Thus the Truth has decreed the narrowness of provision for whoever works in magic, and the Truth always exposes them. A sensible person may say: since they claim success, let them succeed in setting their own affairs right. And since the magician claims that he knows the places of hidden treasures, why does he not find treasures in land that belongs to no one and take them for himself? This is assuming that the magician is extremely trustworthy and does not wish to take from the treasuries of people.

For this reason, you find that all who work in magic and charlatanry die poor, in a wretched state, afflicted in their offspring, because each of them exploited an opportunity that is not available to every one of his human kind, in order to harm people. Read the words of the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted:

﴿And indeed, there were men from mankind who sought refuge with men from the jinn, so they increased them in burden﴾ (Qur'an 72:6).

Here the Truth affirms that they will live in distress and fatigue. Therefore our position on magic is determined: we do not deny it as others deny it. Some scholars have said that the magicians brought staffs into which they put mercury, and when mercury is under the rays of the sun it gives off heat, so the staff writhes. But we do not deny magic, just as we do not deny the jinn, because it is not hidden from us that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "An 'ifrit (a powerful jinn) of the jinn escaped from me last night to cut off my prayer, but Allah, blessed and exalted, enabled me to overpower him, and I wanted to tie him to one of the pillars of the mosque so that all of you might see him in the morning. But I remembered the words of my brother Solomon, peace be upon him: ﴿My Lord, forgive me and grant me a kingdom that will not belong to anyone after me﴾" (1). Since the Truth has said that He created beings you cannot perceive with your senses, we affirm what the Truth has informed us of, because the existence of a thing is one matter, and the perception of its existence is another. Every creature has its own law. The 'ifrit among the jinn said to our master Solomon about the throne of Bilqis: ﴿I will bring it to you before you rise from your place﴾ (Qur'an 27:39). It is as though the jinn sought a period of time, for Solomon might sit in his place with them for an hour or two or three. But the one who had knowledge of the Book said: ﴿I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you﴾ (Qur'an 27:40).

His glance must have returned in less than a second after he said that. This is why the Qur'an reports what happened immediately, saying: ﴿So when he saw it placed before him﴾.

This shows that Allah created the kinds and created for each kind a law. There may be one law stronger than another, but the possessor of a law is himself created, and therefore does not retain it, because the Creator of the law nullifies it and causes the lesser to rule over the greater. Let us reflect on the Qur'anic expression: ﴿They bewitched the eyes of the people﴾.

We are faced with things, namely the staffs and the ropes, and a crowd of humans watching. From His words, ﴿They bewitched the eyes of the people﴾, we understand that the magic falls upon the one who sees it, while the object seen remains in its state: the staffs are the same staffs, the ropes are the same ropes, and what changes is the seer's vision. Therefore He said in another verse:

﴿It was imagined to him, by their magic, that they were moving﴾ (Qur'an 20:66). So magic does not reverse reality; reality remains as it is, and the magician sees it in its true nature. But the people are the ones who see the reality as different. Thus the magicians performed their work, which was: ﴿They bewitched the eyes of the people and frightened them﴾.

"Frightened them" means they put dread into the people's souls through this operation. The magicians supposed that Moses would be afraid like the rest of the bewitched people, and they forgot that Moses would not be deceived by their magic, because through Allah's choosing and His support with the miracle he became a bearer of the law that was sent with him: He made his staff a serpent. And the possessor of the law is the one who controls. They had indeed come with a great magic, which is a logical matter, because the contest was a great contest on which depended the overthrow of Pharaoh's divinity or the preservation of his divinity. Therefore they had to bring the most excellent and greatest of what they possessed of magic.

1 Narrated by al-Bukhari, Muslim and al-Nasa'i.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 7, verse 117:

And the Truth (al-Haqq) says: ﴿And We revealed to Moses: "Throw down your staff," and behold, it swallowed up what they had falsely fabricated.﴾ (7:117)

Why did this matter require a fresh revelation, especially since Moses had already been trained in throwing the staff? We say: there is a difference between teaching in preparation for what will be, and execution at the moment it occurs. At the moment the matter arrives, the Truth issues a new command, for the human nature of Moses may have been touched by something of great magic and terror. And we know that the story of Moses, peace be upon him, contains many wonders. Pharaoh used to kill the males and let the women live, and our Lord, glorified is He, willed that Moses should not be killed, so He said: ﴿And We revealed to the mother of Moses: "Suckle him, and when you fear for him, cast him into the river"﴾ (part of 28:7).

His words ﴿Suckle him, and when you fear for him﴾ indicate that the frightening event has not yet come, but will come later. Bring any woman and tell her: "If you are afraid for your son from some matter, then throw him into the sea." Surely she will not believe you; rather she will mock you, because she will wonder: how can I save him from a presumed death into a certain death? This is the natural course, but here we are before something sent by God to a creature of God, and the sending of God is not contested by doubt. Thus, when the thought and the inspiration come from God, nothing whatsoever competes with them. A person does not ask for proof for it, because his soul has been reassured by it; therefore she cast her infant into the sea before Moses.

God, glorified is He, makes her a mother, and He says: ﴿Do not fear and do not grieve; We will surely return him to you﴾ (part of 28:7), and He did not merely return him to her, but He would entrust to him a great affair: ﴿and We will make him one of the messengers﴾ (part of 28:7). It is as if the Truth, glorified is He, is clarifying to the mother of Moses that her son will not live for her sake alone, but that he has another mission in life, for he will be a messenger from God. If the heavens were not going to preserve him for the sake of the mother's heart and her feelings, then the heavens will preserve him because he has a fundamental mission: ﴿and We will make him one of the messengers﴾. We note that the Truth here did not mention the story of the chest, but in another verse He says: ﴿When We revealed to your mother what was revealed, saying: "Cast him into the chest, then cast it into the sea, and the sea will throw it upon the shore"﴾ (Surah Ta-Ha, 20:38–39).

In this verse He did not say ﴿Do not fear and do not grieve﴾, because He made clear to her what would happen when the sea cast him onto the shore. His words in the first verse ﴿when you fear for him﴾ are a preparation for the event before it comes, while in this verse ﴿When We revealed to your mother what was revealed...﴾ etc., you find quick successive snapshots to express the action at the moment of danger. But in the first verse ﴿Do not fear and do not grieve; We will return him to you and make him one of the messengers﴾, you find slowness, calm and monotony, because it narrates the preparation for what will be.

Thus the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, gives each kind a law, and each law must be respected within its domain, for equality of opportunity among the kinds is what God wills. When God wished to make the matter clear to us, He showed that the believer must look at the givens from behind the obligations. In the verse on debt, for example, you find the Truth enjoining the one who is obligated, the "debtor," who is weak, to write down the debt, and thereby giving an acknowledgment to the creditor, who is strong and capable, so He says: ﴿And do not be weary of writing it, whether small or large, up to its term﴾ (part of 2:282). On the surface the matter seems to protect the creditor and his money, but we must be attentive to the fact that it protects the debtor from himself, because if the debt is not documented, the debtor will not exert the sufficient effort to repay, and through the debtor's striving we benefit existence with an effective energy. But if we do not document the debt, and the debtor grows lax in work and repayment, chaos may spread in society, and every person will refuse to lend to anyone who needs it, and thus economic affairs are corrupted.

Thus, when He commands the documenting of debt, though on the surface it is a protection of the creditor, in its inner reality God protects the debtor, because there is a difference between the moment of bearing the trust and the moment of discharging it.

An example of this: a person comes to you saying, "I have a thousand pounds and I fear losing it, so take it as a trust with you until I need it," and this person has thus deposited a trust with you, and there is no receipt or witnesses, and the matter is left to the trustworthiness of the depositary: if he wishes, he denies; if he wishes, he acknowledges. And you find someone who says to this person: "Hand over what you have." He says this with his obligation and intention that the owner of the thousand pounds, when he comes to ask for it, will give it to him. He promises that at the moment of bearing, but he does not guarantee himself at the moment of discharge, for difficult circumstances may befall him at the time of repayment, and he makes excuses to keep the owner of the money away from him.

Thus there is a difference between the state and readiness of the bearer of the trust at the moment of bearing and at the moment of its discharge. The true believer is one who remembers the moment of bearing and the moment of discharge together; some people refuse to bear a trust in order to remove from themselves the burden of discharging it.

As for one who learns something that contradicts the law of his existence, such as learning magic, we say to him: beware lest you be tested and tempted; rather, keep away, protect yourself, and do not use it. Beware of saying: "I will use what I have learned of magic for good, and whoever comes to me in a crisis, I will resolve it for him by magic." We say to this person: you speak of the time of bearing, but you do not speak of the time of discharge.

The Truth, glorified is He, says: ﴿And We revealed to Moses: "Throw down your staff," and behold, it swallowed up what they had falsely fabricated﴾ (Surah al-A'raf, 7:117). Al-ifk (falsehood) is turning a thing over from its face, and from it comes kadhib (lying). We have known before that every statement has a verbal relation and a factual relation. If you say, for example, "Muhammad is diligent," this is a verbal relation; but is there in reality a person named Muhammad who is trusted in his diligence? If that is so, the verbal relation has agreed with the factual relation, and the statement is truth. As for lying, it is that you say "Muhammad is diligent" when there is no person named Muhammad, or if he exists he is not diligent, and the statement is a lie, because the verbal relation has contradicted the factual relation. When someone lies, he turns the matter over, and we call that kadhib; and the severity of lying is called ifk. Or, kadhib is when there is no correspondence, even if you do not know it; ifk is that you deliberately lie, and this is also fabrication. ﴿that throw down your staff, and behold, it swallows up what they falsely fabricate﴾.

Here the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, says: "fa-idha" (and behold), which expresses suddenness, where the staff of Moses, after it had become a serpent, swallowed what the sorcerers had brought of falsehood and fabrication, and with which they had bewitched the eyes of the people.

Further, He, glorified is He, says after that: ﴿So the truth took place, and what they had been doing was proved void (118)﴾.

His saying ﴿So the truth took place﴾ means: the truth that was theoretical became a tangible reality; for there is a difference between a statement delivered in theory and a statement confirmed by reality. And falling (waqa'a) usually happens from above, so that everyone who sees it recognises it.

And His saying, glorified is He, ﴿So the truth took place﴾ means: the truth was established. Having been a declarative statement that could be affirmed or denied, it became, by its truth, an actual reality. ﴿So the truth took place, and what they had been doing was proved void﴾. What was voided was what they had been doing of sorcery. Indeed, the truth made the truthfulness of Musa (Moses) an observed reality, and by that the sorcerers were overcome.

Allah says: ﴿So they were overcome there and returned humiliated﴾ [7:119].

Not only were the magicians overcome; Pharaoh and his company were also overcome, and everyone who opposed Musa lived in humiliation: the humiliation of the one who summoned and the humiliation of the one who was summoned. Therefore the verse concludes with His words ﴿and returned humiliated﴾, meaning abased.

Almighty Allah then says: ﴿And the magicians were thrown down, prostrating (themselves).﴾

The Truth (ﷺ) did not say, "And the magicians prostrated," but said, "were thrown down" (wa-ulqiya), which indicates that their falling into prostration was not by their own opinion; rather, it was an overwhelming effect (ʿamaliyya infiʿaliyya) of what took place before them, as though something else had thrown them down prostrating, namely the dazzlement by the Truth. The magician among them used to believe that he was the one who was casting the spell. Then the whole company of magicians was taken by surprise: when Moses threw down his staff, they saw it truly become a serpent, and so they knew that the matter was not sorcery. When they threw down their ropes and staves, which they had brought from all the cities (it is said they were loaded onto seventy camels), they witnessed how the staff that had become a living serpent, or a monster (thuʿbān), swallowed all of this and devoured it! The size of the staff remained the size of a staff, however long it became. Thus the magicians became certain that this could not be the work of a magician. Look at their response when they saw it: ﴿They said, "We believe in the Lord of the worlds."﴾

Do they prostrate after belief, or do they believe after prostrating? The text here appears to indicate that they believed after prostrating. Yet the matter required that no one prostrate except because he believed. But we know that belief is an act of the heart, while prostration is a physical act and practical conduct, so each of them believed in his heart and then prostrated.

There is a difference between believing and then prostrating and then declaring their belief, so that they say: "We believe in the Lord of the worlds." Therefore we do not make prostration follow from belief; rather we make prostration accompany the saying of belief and the declaration of belief, because declaring belief is one thing, and belief itself is another thing. So it is as if they believed, then fell down in prostration, and after this they declared their belief, and it is as if the people asked them: "What has happened to you?" And they said: ﴿We believe in the Lord of the worlds﴾.

So whoever tries to find fault with the text must take care to note that their report of belief means the existence of belief first. The sorcerers had believed and then prostrated, so the people were astonished at this prostration, and here the sorcerers said: "Do not be astonished or amazed, for we have believed in the Lord of the worlds." ﴿They said: We believe in the Lord of the worlds﴾ [7:121].

It is said in some exegeses that Pharaoh said: "I am the Lord of the worlds." But the magicians did not leave this claim of his unanswered; they declared that the Lord of the worlds is: ﴿the Lord of Moses and Aaron﴾. And Pharaoh said: "Did I not raise you as a child, Moses?" They replied: "But you did not raise Aaron."

Therefore, Allah here made clear that the Lord of the worlds is: ﴿the Lord of Moses and Aaron﴾ (122).

And because the magicians proclaimed plainly their faith in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Moses and Aaron, Pharaoh was bound to become angry, so the Qur'an brings what came from his own tongue: ﴿Pharaoh said: "Have you believed in Him before I gave you permission? Surely this is a plot you have devised in the city, to drive its people out from it. But you will come to know"﴾ (123).

Pharaoh seems to have still been trying to affirm his authority. We know that the Children of Israel mixed with the people in Egypt, and some of them learned magic. For this reason, Pharaoh accused the magicians of having agreed with Moses on this matter.

Pharaoh was in a predicament and wanted to extricate himself from it, because all the people had witnessed the matter, and he did not want them to begin doubting his divinity, lest the edifice he had erected on lies collapse. So he said to the magicians: "Indeed, this is a scheme you have plotted in the city," meaning that you have colluded with Moses. Later he would say, accusing Moses: ﴿Indeed, he is your chief who taught you magic﴾ (part of verse 71 of Surah Ta-Ha). As a result of this supposed scheming between the Children of Israel and Moses, Pharaoh threatens them: ﴿I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides, then I will crucify you all﴾ (124).

The threat, as we see it, is harsh and dreadful; cutting off hands and feet and then crucifixion are all things that frighten.

What then is the response of those who receive this threat, when the cheerfulness of faith has mingled with their hearts? They say: ﴿Indeed, to our Lord we are returning.﴾ [Qur'an 7:125]

You have hastened for us the good, for we shall be in the neighborhood of our Lord. So you, by your recklessness and foolishness, have done us a favor and a good you did not intend.

They add to Pharaoh's rebuke with what comes in the Qur'an on their tongues: ﴿And you resent us only because we believed in the signs of our Lord when they came to us. Our Lord, pour upon us patience, and cause us to die as Muslims.﴾

"What you resent from us" — because "tanqim" means to resent or dislike. Their words to Pharaoh amount to: Is it not that what you dislike in us is that we believed in the signs of our Lord when they came to us? Yet is believing in the signs of God, when they arrive, something that is disliked?! In the language this is called "ta'kid al-madh bi-ma yushbih al-dhamm" (emphasis of praise through what resembles blame), as when a person says: What do you dislike in me? My honesty? My generosity? My knowledge?

It is as if he were enumerating things that everyone knows in reality are not disliked, but the fault lies in the scale of values: it is those who dislike what is right. These are matters that do not deserve to be disliked, censured, or blamed. They were certain that meeting God in faith is good, and every one of them prefers the neighbourhood of God over the neighbourhood of Pharaoh. What Pharaoh regards as punishment in fact establishes his failure even in anticipating punishment, for if he did not threaten them with this death, they would still die and return to God, and this is an absolute certainty, since every creature's destiny is to return to God. It is as though they nullified Pharaoh's threat when he said to them:

﴿I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides, then I will surely crucify you all﴾ (Surah al-A'raf). Then they turn to their Lord and Creator and say: ﴿Our Lord, pour upon us patience, and cause us to die as Muslims.﴾ "Ifragh" means that something is poured over something to cover it entirely. It is as if they were saying: Give us, O Lord, all patience, for we need patience because Pharaoh has threatened that he will cut off our hands and feet. For this reason, one of the knowers of God said: "I marvel at Pharaoh's sorcerers: at the beginning of the day they were disbelieving sorcerers, and at the end of the day they were righteous martyrs."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 7, verse 127:

He, glorified is He, says: ﴿The chiefs of the people of Pharaoh said, "Will you leave Moses and his people to spread corruption in the land and abandon you and your gods?" He said, "We will kill their sons and spare their women, and we are dominant over them."﴾

Thus we learn that the nobles closest to Pharaoh were the first to fear for their rule. This statement also indicates that Pharaoh had not yet touched Moses with any harm, for he was still living in the awe of certainty and the force of truth, which made him anxious and fearful of Moses. Pharaoh was the first to know that his claim to divinity was entirely false, and he knew well that Moses was in the right, but announcing his defeat before the assembly is not an easy matter for the human soul. The chiefs of Pharaoh's people, before whom his authority and standing had been shaken, asked him: "Will you leave Moses and his people to spread corruption in the land?" Or, as it appears, Moses and Aaron had left the place after they had finished with the matter of the magicians, and Pharaoh had not seized them; therefore the chiefs of Pharaoh's people asked: ﴿The chiefs of the people of Pharaoh said, "Will you leave Moses and his people to spread corruption in the land and abandon you and your gods?"﴾ (part of verse 127, Surah al-A'raf). "Yadharaka" means he leaves you and abandons you. Pharaoh believed that there were gods of the heights and gods of the lowers, and that he was the lord of the entire lower world. Therefore they said: ﴿and abandon you and your gods﴾. There is another reading, "wa yadharaka ilahatak," meaning worship of you, i.e., he abandons you and abandons your worship.

Pharaoh says: ﴿He said, "We will kill their sons and spare their women."﴾

Up to that moment Pharaoh had not touched Moses, and his fear of Moses still prevents him from approaching him, drawing near to him, or contacting him even with a word. He takes care not to undertake anything against Moses, lest Moses surprise him with a second surprise. It is said that the serpent which appeared at the moment Moses cast his staff opened its jaws and turned toward Pharaoh, and he said: "Restrain it from me, and I will believe in what you have brought." This is a plausible matter, because Pharaoh up to this moment had not dared to approach Moses, and he brought up the news of killing the sons and enslaving the women, but did not bring up the conduct of Moses. ﴿We will kill their sons and spare their women, and we are dominant over them﴾ (part of verse 127, Surah al-A'raf).

The strong, when he possesses power over the weak, does not tighten the noose upon him in order to devour him, because he knows his weakness and can reach him at any time; but if the opponent before you is strong, you terrify him with force until he submits to you. Here Pharaoh says: ﴿and we are dominant over them﴾:

Pharaoh assures his people that they are in control and dominant, and that the people of Moses will not be able to escape them. Pharaoh affirms: "We will kill their sons and spare their women," because the sons are the military strength, and women's customary condition is based on veiling and concealment; and sparing the women while killing the men is a humiliation of the men, since the toil will fall to the women. For this reason, when the Arabs raided an enemy, they would bring their women along to increase zeal, so that no one would weaken or act cowardly; you would see a man's wife, sister, or daughter with him in that state. Likewise the Arabs feared defeat, lest the enemy seize their women and take them as captives.

Here Pharaoh affirms his insistence on humiliating the people of Moses by repeating the killing of the sons and the sparing of the women. Pharaoh had done the same before. The reason is that the Children of Israel had been assisting the kings of the Hyksos; after the Pharaohs expelled the Hyksos, they turned to harming the Children of Israel, who had been on the Hyksos' side, and whoever remained of the Children of Israel was subjected to the killing of sons. But the Truth saved Moses when He inspired his mother to cast him into the river so that Pharaoh would raise him. And here is Pharaoh repeating the attempt, by commanding the killing of sons and the enslavement of women.

Almighty Allah then says: ﴿Moses said to his people, "Seek help in Allah and be patient. Indeed, the earth belongs to Allah; He gives it as inheritance to whom He wills of His servants. And the good outcome is for the righteous (al-muttaqun)."﴾

Moses affirms the clear truth, which is that the earth does not belong to Pharaoh, and that the good outcome belongs only to the righteous. It is as if, by this statement, he wants to bring them back to the judgment of history, where the good outcome is not always for the righteous. Pharaoh had said: "And indeed we are above them, dominant, prevailing, overpowering, in control." Moses responds to that: "I seek help from One who is stronger than you." Moses, peace be upon him, commands his people to seek help in Allah and to be patient over what befalls them of Pharaoh's oppression and tyranny.

Because the people of Moses were among the oppressed, God promised that He would grant them security in the land and establish them in it. This is a report from God, and God's reports are certainties. But what was the response of the people of Moses to this great victory of Moses, and to their own victory?

We find the Truthful One, glorified is He, saying: ﴿They said: "We were harmed before you came to us and after you came to us." He said: "It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land, and then see how you act."﴾ (7:129)

They said to Moses: "We were harmed before you came to us, when they slaughtered our sons and spared our women. And after you came, here we are, still suffering harm." It was as if his coming had done nothing for them. So they looked only at the trials that God sends upon His creatures, and did not look at the favour, the gift and the bounty, nor at the blessings of victory, nor at the fact that Pharaoh had mustered all his sorcerers and then Moses defeated them. It should have been a reminder to them of the measure of God's gifts. They counted the days of affliction and did not count the days of ease.

His words ﴿then see how you act﴾ indicate that they would break their covenants and do things that do not fit with these foundations. In Islamic history, we find that 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd entered upon al-Mansur before he became Commander of the Faithful. There was in front of him one loaf or two loaves, and he said: "Find a loaf for the son of 'Ubayd." The attendant replied: "We cannot find one." When al-Mansur assumed the caliphate and lived in the wealth and luxury of kingship, Ibn 'Ubayd entered upon him and said: "The Truth has spoken rightly to you, O Commander of the Faithful, in His saying: ﴿It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land, and then see how you act﴾ (part of 7:129)." Moses said this to his people after they reproached him for his inability to turn away the punishment from them.

Thus the people of Moses received the first defeat of Pharaoh at the hands of Moses, and they said to him: "We were harmed before you came to us and after you came to us," meaning by slaughter, sparing of women and killing of sons. It was as if your coming had not benefited us at all, because we remain in the torment that we have been suffering. So we have no need of you, and there is no necessity for your presence, as evidenced by the fact that what happens after you is what happened before you.

They did not consider that harm, before and after, arises only from an enemy. So it is as if Moses replied to them that the causes of harm will end, and that God will destroy your enemy who harmed you before and who harms you after. The matter will not be limited to this blessing; rather, He will increase you by making you successors in the land, giving you their kingdom and giving you their land. Here there are two matters. The first is negative: the destruction of the enemy. The second is positive: your being made successors in the land. This is a command to you and a promise from God that sovereignty and kingship will be yours. You must pay attention to God's blessing upon you in the destruction of your enemy and in your being made successors in the land. You will not be left as you are; rather, I am watching over you, to see what you do. Will you receive these blessings with gratitude, increased faith, certainty and attachment to God, or will you disbelieve in this blessing?

When the Truthful One, glorified and exalted is He, says on the tongue of Moses ﴿'asā (it may be that)﴾, it is a word which, as the linguists say, indicates hope. The meaning of hope is that what follows it is something hoped for. There is a difference between tamannī (wishing) and rajā' (hoping). Wishing is to seek something impossible, or something whose attainment is difficult, but by wishing you only want to express your love for it. If you say: "Would that youth would return," this will not happen, but you are declaring your love for the stage of youth. The most that it gives is to inform us that you love what is wished for. As for whether it will come about or not, this is not in question.

But rajā' (hope) is something beloved that is about to happen. Thus we know that hope is stronger than wishing. The particle of wishing is layta (would that), and the particle of hope is 'asā (perhaps). When what is hoped for follows 'asā, there are stages that differ in the strength of the causes of the hope being fulfilled. For example, if I say: "'Asā an ukrimaka (perhaps I will honour you)," this matter depends on me, because my honouring you requires that I remain, and that my disposition towards you does not change. It is possible that my disposition may change before I honour you, and then my honouring you does not occur. This is the hope of one who is subject to changes, and as long as I am subject to changes, I may not be able to honour you, or I may be able but no longer wish to do so because my soul has turned away from it. This spoils the hope and lessens the expectation of its fulfilment. If you say to someone: "'Asā an yukrimaka Fulān (perhaps Fulan will honour you)," and Fulan is his equal, then this is somewhat unlikely, because the one who speaks in this way cannot be sure that Fulan will honour his equal, since Fulan too is subject to changes.

But if you say: "'Asā Allāh an yukrimaka (perhaps God will honour you)," this is stronger, because our Lord is not incapable of honouring any person. Yet will God accept to answer your hope? This is a matter that requires pause. Glorified is He: in terms of power, He has absolute capability, so nothing hinders Him, nothing resists Him, and nothing refuses Him. So when the Truth says about Himself ﴿'asā rabbukum (perhaps your Lord)﴾, the matter is settled, the promise is decided and fulfilled, and this is what is called certain hope. Thus the stages of hope are: "'Asā an ukrimaka (perhaps I will honour you)," "'Asā an yukrimaka Zayd (perhaps Zayd will honour you)," "'Asā Allāh an yukrimaka (perhaps God will honour you)," and the strongest forms of hope are when the Truth promises honour or mercy.

﴿It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy﴾ (part of 7:129). The speech, as we see, is from Moses, and no one can bring about this matter except God. So what is the place of this in the fulfilment of the hope? We know that Moses is a messenger whom God sent to guide creation, and He sent him supported by a miracle. If a messenger supported by a miracle has been commanded by God to convey this to them, then his hope is accepted: ﴿It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy﴾.

Sometimes the removal of a harmful thing is a blessing by itself. But that God should destroy my enemy and give me the rights of my enemy's high station is a blessing of bestowal that comes after a blessing of removal. Something similar will happen on the Day of Resurrection, because the Truth says: ﴿Whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted to the Garden has indeed triumphed﴾ (part of 3:185). Mere removal from the Fire is a favour and a blessing, so what of one who is removed from the Fire and admitted to the Garden?

He has received two blessings. Here the Truthful One, glorified is He, says: ﴿It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy﴾. That alone is a blessing, followed by another blessing: ﴿and make you successors in the land﴾. But the price of these blessings is that He will see how you act. Will you thank these blessings and be righteous servants, or will you deny and disbelieve in them? Indeed, man is wrongdoing and ungrateful.

When the word "yanzur (He sees/looks)" is applied to a human being, its meaning is understood, namely that he sees you with his eye. When it is attributed to God, the matter is different, for God is exalted above having a pupil of the eye like our eyes. Glorified is He: He does not need to know anything in order to look at it, because He knew it before it occurred. We know that there is a difference between judging a creature by the knowledge of the Creator and judging a creature by the deeds of the creature.

An example of this: a professor in a subject knows the levels of the students who study under him. The dean says to him: "What is your opinion?" He says: "This one is a student who deserves success with high marks, and the second will surely fail." The professor says this judgement on the basis of his knowledge of each student's condition. But if the professor fails a student on the basis of his assessment without an examination, the student who failed may say to his teacher: "You have been unjust in your judgement; if you had let me sit the examination, I would have passed." When the dean decides to examine the student, and the examination takes place in fact, but the student fails, it then becomes clear to the dean that the professor's judgement that the student would fail was known first, and then the student's failure in the examination followed.

When God, glorified is He, says ﴿then see how you act﴾, He does not look in order to know it, far be it from God, for He knows it; rather, He does not want to judge His creatures by His knowledge, but He wants to judge His creatures by the deeds of His creatures. Glorified is He, He has eternally known everyone who will be guided and everyone who will go astray. For this reason He created the Garden and created the Fire, each able to contain all creation, and He did not create places in the Garden only in proportion to those who will enter it, nor did He create places in the Fire that could hold only the people of the Fire; rather, it can contain all creation. He did not judge by His knowledge in this matter, but leaves the final judgement to the reality of things, as long as there is choice for man. Supposing you all believed, you would all have places in the Garden. And supposing, God forbid, you disbelieved, you would have places in the Fire. He, glorified is He, will not create anything new, rather He has prepared everything and the matter is concluded.

When the people of the Garden come to enter the Garden, and the people of the Fire, there will be for the people of the Garden other seats that had been allotted to those who entered the Fire. And it will be announced to the people of the Garden: "Inherit it and take it yourselves": ﴿And they will be called: "This is the Garden which you have inherited"﴾ (part of 7:43). It is an inheritance from those for whom it had been prepared but who did not do the deeds that would qualify them to possess it. So beware lest you understand that God's looking at His creatures is in order to learn something from them. No. He is the All-Knowing from eternity.

Therefore the Truthful One, glorified and exalted is He, says: ﴿And that God may know who supports Him and His messengers unseen﴾ (part of 57:25). Glorified is He: He knows eternally, and His knowledge of people's actions becomes realised in the reality of their conduct, and the knowledge of reality is what constitutes proof against creation. Here, in the verse under discussion, there are three things: that God, glorified is He, will destroy your enemy, that He will make you successors in the land, and then He will see how you act. Let us examine which of these two has been realised.
