Regarding this, the Messenger of God said: "I have been given five things that none before me was given: I was made victorious with terror over a distance of a month's journey; the earth has been made for me a place of prostration and a means of purification, so whoever of my community is overtaken by the prayer, let him pray; spoils of war have been made lawful for me, whereas a prophet used to be sent to his own people only, but I have been sent to all people; and I have been given intercession" (1). Then, after that, the Divine, glorified and exalted, wished to establish the universality of the message through the universality of the subjugation of the cosmos to creation. Therefore the address was directed to all people: ﴿Say: O mankind﴾. And everyone who is called "people," to them the Messenger is sent: ﴿I am the Messenger of God to you all﴾. He, glorified be He, wished to give us the grounds that make God a Messenger who conveys to his people and to all nations the method of God for the movement of their lives, so He said: ﴿To whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾.

Since He is the One who possesses the heavens and the earth, and no one among His creatures has claimed that he possesses them, and in the heavens and the earth and what is between them is our life and the essentials of our existence, He, glorified be He, is more fitting and more worthy to be worshipped. Had the sky belonged to one, and the air to one, and the earth to one, and what is between them to one, it would have been possible for there to be a god here, and a god there, and a god yonder. Regarding this the Divine says: ﴿Then each god would have gone off with what he created, and some of them would have overcome others﴾ (from 23:91). Thus, since the whole existence, from the heavens and the earth and what is other than them, is under the dominion of God, He is the most fitting to be worshipped, and the foremost peak of worship is to bear witness that there is no god but God, and the primary ground of His divinity is that to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. And since He is a god, He must be obeyed, but only through a method, and there is no method except "do" and "do not." And the foremost of the method, the summit of belief, is monotheism (tawhid). God has made for monotheism a ground drawn from the reality of life, so He said: ﴿He gives life and causes death﴾. This is a matter that no one has ever claimed, because God is the One to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and because He gives life and causes death. For this reason we find that the one who disputed with Abraham about his Lord, concerning whom the Divine says: ﴿When God had given him the kingdom, when Abraham said, "My Lord is He who gives life and causes death"﴾ (from 2:258). This king tried to conduct a misleading sophistical argument in order to confound and silence Abraham, peace be upon him, so he said: ﴿I give life and cause death﴾ (from 2:258): namely, by ordering a person killed and then pardoning him, and by that, in the logic of the sophists, he is not causing death but giving life. But is ordering a killing the same as death? Of course not; for there is a difference between death and killing. A person may kill another person, but he cannot cause his death, because death comes without anything destroying its structure, whether a bullet, a stone, or a bomb. No one is able to cause someone's death if he wishes to cause it; death is what occurs without a cause. But that one person kills another is possible, and therefore the Divine says of Himself: ﴿He gives life and causes death, so believe in God and His Messenger﴾ (from 7:157).

Observe the precision of the expression: since the Divine has commanded His Messenger to say, "I am the Messenger of God to you all," and the ground of faith is the affirmation and conviction in the unity of the God to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, who is there is no god but Him, and who gives life and causes death, therefore He calls them to belief in the Supreme Creator: ﴿So believe in God and His Messenger﴾.

He did not say "Muhammad, and believe in me," because it is not a matter of your personal self, O Muhammad; rather it is an honoring of your message to people. Belief is not in your essence and person, but because you are the Messenger of God. So He brought the original ground: ﴿So believe in God and His Messenger﴾, and the Messenger may be Muhammad or other than Muhammad. Then after that He described the Prophet: ﴿the unlettered Prophet who believes in God and His words﴾. Unlettered-ness, as we have learned before, is an honor for our master Muhammad (ﷺ), and he (ﷺ) believes in the words of God, which are either what has reached us of his manner of the Qur'an, or what Moses said to his people: ﴿And make my speech in his mouth﴾ (see 20:27–28).

And of Jesus it is said that he does not speak from himself, but the words of our Lord come to him in his mouth. The comprehensive statement describing the words of Muhammad (ﷺ) is what the Divine clarified in His saying: ﴿Nor does he speak from desire﴾ (Surah al-Najm). Or the belief in the words means that one believes that every existent of God's creation was created by a word from Him: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ (Surah Ya-Sin, 36:82).

Someone may say: how does God address a thing that did not yet exist? We say: He, glorified be He, has known it from eternity, and its existence is established and fixed. But God wishes to bring this existent forth to people. The existence of any thing is eternal in God's knowledge, and it is as if He says to the thing: "Appear, O being, into existence, that people may see you, after you had been buried within the folds of My power."

Whether the word is by creating causes, like the creation of the sun and the moon, or by creating a thing without causes, like Jesus, peace be upon him, who is "a word from Him," that is, a word that transcended the scope of causes, in that our lady Mary bore him without a man. In this there is a transcending of causes, and therefore the Divine, glorified be He, said: ﴿a word from Him﴾. We know that everything comes to be only by a word from Him, glorified be He, but by a word that has causes, or by a word that has no causes. The words are also the signs in which lie the method of the rulings, and therefore the Divine's saying comes: ﴿Say: We believe in God, and in what has been sent down to us, and what was sent down to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the Tribes, and what was given to Moses and Jesus, and what was given to the prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we submit﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 2:136).

And a narration tells us that our master Moses, peace be upon him, said to his Lord: "I find in the Tablets a community who believe in the first Book and the last Book, and who fight the rulers of error until they fight the one-eyed liar; so make them my community." He said: "That is the community of Aḥmad" (2).

And Moses's saying "believe in the first Book and the last Book" is what is indicated by the Divine's saying:

﴿Say: We believe in God, and in what has been sent down to us, and what was sent down to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the Tribes﴾ (from 2:136).

The Divine concludes the verse we are reflecting upon with His saying:

﴿and follow him that you may be guided﴾. "La'alla" (perhaps/that you may) signifies hope and request. We know that every request concerns one of two matters: either a request for the impossible, which you make to show that you love it, a kind of wishing, like the saying of one who says: "Would that youth returned one day," for he knows that youth does not return, but he says it to make you feel that he loves youth; or like a person's saying: "Would that the stars drew near to me so I might string them into necklaces of praise," which is a request for the impossible, but he wishes to make you feel that this is something he loves. And the other is a request that can be realized, and this is what is called hope (raja'). It has stages: when you hope for something for a person, you say: "Perhaps so-and-so will give you such-and-such." And entering into the category of hope, you say: "Perhaps I will give you," because the hope is from you, and you are the one who says it, and yet you may not be able to fulfill it; and the stronger form is to say: "Perhaps God will give you." But these are from your words, so God may respond to you or may not respond. As for when God says "la'allakum" (perhaps you), this is the most certain of hopes, and it must be realized.

(1) Agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayh).
(2) Ibn Kathir, in his commentary on the Divine's saying: "And when the anger ceased from Moses…"

Whenever the Truth speaks about the people of Musa (Moses), He speaks of them by presenting their stories, their disgraceful conduct, and their breaking of the covenant despite the vast and abundant blessings of Allah upon them. And He made clear to us: beware that you take this ruling as general, for if the ruling were general, there would not have been found among the nation of Musa anyone who believes in Muhammad. For this reason we have said in the past that there is what is called "preservation of possibility" (ṣiyānat al-iḥtimāl). An example of this: we find among the Jews those who believed in the message of the Messenger of Allah, such as Mukhayriq, of whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Mukhayriq is the best of the Jews." And ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam... Indeed, some of the Jews were preoccupied with the question of faith, and therefore the matter is not to be taken as a general ruling, for among the people of Musa are those whom the Truth describes with noble words:

﴿And among the people of Musa is a community who guide by the truth and by it act justly.﴾ [7:159].

When the people of Musa hear this statement, they will say to themselves that He knows what is in our hearts of thinking about believing in the message of Muhammad (ﷺ). But if the ruling were generalized, whoever is considering belief in Muhammad would say: Why does He issue a ruling against me while I am contemplating belief? But the Truth has "preserved the possibility" and made clear to each one of those who are considering belief in Muhammad (ﷺ) that he should move toward declaring faith, so He said:

﴿And among the people of Musa is a community who guide by the truth and by it act justly.﴾ (Surat al-A'raf).

That is, they guide people to the truth and call them to the path of goodness, and by this truth they act justly in judging between people and do not deviate.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 7, verse 160:

Then the Truth (al-Haqq) says:

﴿And We divided them into twelve tribes, as nations. And We inspired to Moses, when his people asked him for water: "Strike the rock with your staff." And there gushed forth from it twelve springs. Every people knew its drinking place. And We shaded them with clouds and sent down upon them manna and quails: "Eat of the good things with which We have provided you." And they did not wrong Us, but they used to wrong themselves.﴾ (160)

When the Truth says "qatta'nahum" (We divided them), this returns to the people of Moses. We know that the Qur'an does not, as other books do, devote one section to Moses, another to Jesus and a third to Muhammad. No, it makes the method of faith one single dough in the call: it brings the matter of Jesus, then enters into the call the matter of Moses and others, and so on, then returns to the original subject, so as to exploit the emotions of the soul after any story of the stories.

Here the Truth, glorified be He, returns to the people of Moses once more. Having been fair to them, and having shown that among them is a nation who guide by the truth and by it act justly, He says: ﴿And We divided them into twelve tribes, as nations.﴾ The intended meaning here is the Children of Israel. The meaning of "qatta'tu al-shay'" (I cut the thing) is that the thing had a complete existence together with its parts; then you cut it and separate some of it from others, and make it into pieces and parts. They are all the Children of Israel, but the Truth makes clear that He divided them and made them "asbat" (tribes). The "sibt" is the son's son (grandson), and here they are the sons of our master Ya'qub (Jacob), who were twelve sons. Surah Yusuf relates and says: ﴿O my father, indeed I saw eleven stars and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me.﴾ (Qur'an 12:4)

When you count and enumerate, you will find eleven visible stars; add to them the sun, the moon and the seer, and the number becomes fourteen. Leave out the sun and the moon, because they symbolise Ya'qub and his wife; take the eleven stars and add the seer, who is Yusuf, and the number is twelve. These are the twelve tribes. Our master Ya'qub had twelve sons from different mothers, and we know from before that when mothers are many, the inclinations of desire among the children may conflict. For this reason our master Ya'qub foresaw and said to our master Yusuf: ﴿Do not relate your vision to your brothers, lest they plot against you a plot.﴾ (Qur'an 12:5). This is the first proof that they differed, and it is one of the causes and grounds of the division: ﴿And We divided them into twelve tribes.﴾ In Surah Yusuf we read: ﴿This is the interpretation of my vision from before; my Lord has made it true.﴾ (Qur'an 12:100)

Here the Truth, glorified be He, says: ﴿And We inspired to Moses, when his people asked him for water: "Strike with your staff the rock," and there gushed forth from it twelve springs.﴾ (Qur'an 7:160)

They did not even want mere sharing of the water, anticipating disagreement among themselves. So the Truth gave each tribe a spring from which to drink, to treat what was in them of the ailments of jealousy and resentment toward one another; for the Truth said of them: ﴿And We divided them into twelve tribes, as nations.﴾

Here is a linguistic pause only: the "asbat" among the sons of Ya'qub and Ishaq correspond to the "qaba'il" (tribes) among the sons of Isma'il. The sons of Isma'il, the Arabs, are called qaba'il, and these are called "asbat." We know that the word "ithnata" (two, feminine) indicates that they are feminine, and "'ashara" (ten) is also feminine, because we say: "Two men came to me" (rajulan ithnan) and "two women came to me" (imra'atan ithnatan); that is, ithnan for males and ithnatan for females. The compound "ithnata 'ashara" (twelve) is a compound number whose specification (tamyiz) is always singular, and for this reason the Truth says: ﴿eleven stars.﴾

So "ithnata 'ashara" indicates the feminine. But the mentioned term here is "sibt," and "sibt" is masculine. We may note that when it is pluralised it becomes feminine, since they say: "Every plural is feminine." Also, the intended meaning of "asbat" is the tribes, whose singular is "qabila," which is feminine. Their being cut off means that previously they had a unity that gathered them, so the Truth wanted to draw our attention to the fact that they are of one thing. He brought the word "asbat" in place of "qabila," and the singular "qabila" is feminine; one says "twelve tribes" (ithnata 'ashara qabilah), and one does not say "twelve tribes" (ithnata 'ashara qaba'il). He placed "asbat" in the position of "qabila," because each qabila includes asbat; therefore the specification came in the masculine.

﴿And We divided them into twelve tribes, as nations.﴾ (Qur'an 7:160)

That is, We made each sibt a nation in its own right. The cosmic reality has proven that they are so, because you do not find among them in past times a national gathering, which is what they call "the National Homeland for the Jews," although the unjust powerful states aided them and established for them a homeland on the land of Palestine. Nevertheless, in every country you find a group of them living isolated from the peoples in whose midst they live, as though they do not want to dissolve into the peoples. In Paris, for example, you find "the Jewish quarter," and in London the matter is the same; in every large city this story is repeated. They live in them with their rituals, their appearance, their food and their customs, isolated from the peoples, as though they are carrying out God's decree concerning them: ﴿And We divided them into twelve tribes, as nations.﴾

Our Lord divided them in the earth, that is, He dispersed them in the lands and did not give them an independent homeland. For this reason you will read in Surah al-Isra', God willing: ﴿And We said after him to the Children of Israel: "Dwell in the land."﴾ (Qur'an 17:104)

That is, He, glorified be He, said to them after Moses: "Dwell in the land." When you say to us, "O Lord, let him dwell," you specify a place on earth, such as a person dwelling in Alexandria or Cairo or Jordan or Syria. But that the judgement is issued that "Dwell in the land" means that they should scatter throughout it, so there is no collective gathering for you.

The Truth says: ﴿So when the promise of the Hereafter comes, We will bring you forth as a mixed multitude.﴾ (Qur'an 17:104)

That is, when the promise of the Hereafter comes, it will be a decisive blow upon you, O Jews, because your enemy will not pursue you in every nation, nor send an army to fight you in every place where a group of you lives. But when the promise of the Hereafter comes, the Truth will bring them as a mixed multitude, and they will gather. In this "national homeland" in which they rejoice, we say to them: do not rejoice, for this is the gathering of which God said: "We bring you as a mixed multitude," so that the blow may be directed at you in one place, to uproot and destroy you.

Then the Truth brings the report of the miracles: ﴿And We inspired to Moses, when his people asked him for water, "Strike the rock with your staff."﴾ (Qur'an 7:160)

"Istasqa" (asked for water) means to request irrigation (suqya), and suqya is the request for water which removes thirst from a person. Since they asked for suqya, they must have been suffering from thirst, as though they were in the wilderness. God, glorified be He, wanted to show them His blessing at the time of need; He left them until they became thirsty so that they would ask, and so that they would feel the blessing of quenching.

The Truth says: ﴿when his people asked him for water﴾, that is, they asked Moses to ask God for water. Why did they turn to Moses at the time of thirst? Moses said to them: "It is not by my own self that I quench you, but I will ask my Lord to give you drink for you." We know that the constituents of life, in the necessary existential order, are: air, water and food. Whenever you see a hamza, a sin and a ta' attached to something, know that it is a matter sought and desired.

An example of this: when Moses and the righteous servant travelled and came to a town and "istat'amā" (asked its people for food), that is, they requested food, and this is the third constituent of life. Here "istasqa" means requesting the second constituent, which is water, and we know that the first constituent, which is air, we cannot do without. Therefore God did not place it in anyone's hand, but gave it and bestowed it upon all creation.

And since air is not owned and is common, this process did not occur with it. Rather, food can be owned, and water can be owned, so He said once "istat'ama" and here "istasqa"; and "istahwa" (to ask for air) was not found. But "istahwa" in the Qur'an means to seek to make someone follow one's desire: ﴿like one whom the devils have enticed (istahwat-hu al-shayatin)﴾ (Qur'an 6:71), that is, the devils sought to make his desire and aim follow what they wanted, not what God wants.

The story of the asking for water has come before in Surah al-Baqarah: ﴿And when Moses asked for water for his people.﴾ In Surah al-A'raf, which is the subject of our reflections, it is they who asked for water. Is there a contradiction? Of course not; because the people of Moses asked Moses for water, and he asked his Lord for water for them. Is this repetition? No; because He, glorified be He, spoke here about the intermediary, and afterwards spoke about the origin, which is He, glorified be He, the giver of water; so here He said: "when his people asked him," and in Surah al-Baqarah He said: ﴿And when Moses asked for water for his people.﴾

This is a natural order. I say this so that we know the difference between the two expressions, to confirm that there is neither disagreement nor repetition; because the one asking here is the people, the ones for whom water is asked are Moses, and the one from whom it is asked is God, majestic is His power, and this is a natural matter.

And the Truth, glorified be He, says in Surah al-Baqarah:

﴿And when Moses asked for water for his people, We said: "Strike with your staff the rock."﴾ (Qur'an 2:60)

We find the inspiration came to Moses with His words: ﴿We said, "Strike."﴾ And here in Surah al-A'raf we find the Truth saying: ﴿And We inspired to Moses, when his people asked him for water, "Strike with your staff the rock."﴾ (Qur'an 7:160)

We should know that "qulna" (We said) is exactly equal to "awhayna" (We inspired), because the intended meaning of speech here is not the category of God's speaking to Moses; rather, the category of this matter is different from His words, the Truth:

﴿And God spoke to Moses directly.﴾ (Qur'an 4:164)

So not every inspiration to Moses came by direct speech from God; rather, He spoke to him once as an honour, then inspired to him afterwards like the other messengers.

And His words, the Truth: ﴿that strike with your staff the rock, and there gushed forth from it twelve springs.﴾ (Qur'an 7:160)

This statement indicates to us absolute miraculousness. Once the Truth commanded Moses to strike the water with the staff, ﴿so it split, and each part was like a great mountain﴾ (Qur'an 26:63); and once here He commands him to strike the rock, from which water gushes. Thus we see the absolute power of God, who gives and withholds by one thing, and this was only by the means in God's hand, which He moves as He wills. For this reason we saw God's command when Moses struck the sea with his staff, so that each part became like a mountain, that is, like a mountain, and fluidity was prevented. When Moses and his people went out to the dry land after crossing the sea, he wanted to strike the sea so that it would return again to its former state of flow, but God inspired to him: "Leave the sea as a calm (rahwan)."

That is, leave it as it is; for God wanted Pharaoh and his people to be deceived into seeing the dry land as a path existing between the water, so they would attempt to pass through it behind Moses and his people. But as soon as Pharaoh and his people entered behind Moses, the water returned to its flow and drowned Pharaoh and his people. Thus God saved and drowned by one thing; and likewise in the matter of the staff: it, when it struck the water, split it so that each part became like a mountain and a towering hill, then Moses struck the rock with it and there gushed from it twelve springs of water. Thus we see the power of Him in whose hand are power and means.

﴿Strike with your staff the rock, and there gushed forth from it twelve springs.﴾ (Qur'an 7:160)

Here is the expression "infajarat" (gushed/burst forth), and there the expression "infajarat" (burst forth). We know that "inbijas" (oozing) occurs first, then "infijar" (bursting) follows second; "inbijas" is that the water comes drop by drop, then "infijar" comes and abundant waters flow out. So it was

Then the Truth (exalted is He) says:

﴿And when it was said to them: "Dwell in this town and eat from it wherever you wish, and say: 'Remission,' and enter the gate prostrating; We shall forgive you your sins, and We shall increase the good-doers [in reward]."﴾ (7:161)

This story is also mentioned in Surah al-Baqarah. We know that His saying (exalted is He): ﴿And when it was said to them﴾ does not mention who the speaker was, because the nature of the matter concerning the Tribes (al-Asbat) is that He (exalted is He) made for each tribe among them a spring from which it drinks, and each tribe had a chief (naqib). This is evidence that they do not gather into one unity, so the saying does not proceed from one to all; rather, the saying proceeds from the Supreme Legislator, who is the Truth, to the Messenger, and the Messenger says it to the chiefs (nuqaba'), and the chiefs say it to the people.

After Moses received the saying, he conveyed it to the chiefs, and the chiefs said it to the Tribes. In another verse the Truth said: ﴿And when We said﴾. This first saying places before us a snapshot showing that the original source of the saying is God; and since they are Tribes and each tribe has its own watering place, the Truth here clarifies that it was revealed to Moses. Whenever you hear "wa-idh" (and when), know that the intended meaning is: "Remember when it was said to them: Dwell in this town." It has been said that this town is Bayt al-Maqdis or Jericho, but they said: "We will never enter it, for in it are tyrannical people," and they added: ﴿So go you and your Lord and fight, for we are sitting here﴾ (5:24).

The Truth does not specify the town in this verse, because that is an unimportant matter; rather He brought the important point, which has its weight and significance, namely the execution of the command in whatever place it may be: ﴿Dwell in this town and eat from it﴾.

The Truth clarifies: I have undertaken for you therein, just as I undertook for you in the wilderness, with the shading of clouds, the gushing of water from rock, and manna and quail. When I tell you to enter the town and dwell in it, I will not abandon you: ﴿and eat from it wherever you wish﴾. Since a town had a gate in ancient times, He (exalted is He) continues: ﴿and say: "Remission," and enter the gate prostrating﴾.

"Hittah" means the supplication that they say: "O Lord, remove from us our sins, for we have complied with Your command and have come to the town that You ordered us to dwell in." It was incumbent upon them to enter it prostrating, because God had saved them from the wilderness after bestowing favour upon them and granting them ease therein. If they do this, their reward will be: ﴿We shall forgive you your sins, and We shall increase the good-doers [in reward]﴾ (7:161). He (exalted is He) forgives once and then records a good deed, meaning the removal of harm and the bringing of benefit. But there, in Surah al-Baqarah, the following text has come:

﴿And when We said: Enter this town and eat from it wherever you wish, in abundance, and enter the gate prostrating and say "Hittah"; We shall forgive you your sins and We shall increase the good-doers (2:58)﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah).

The general structure is one, and we find differences in the wording and images from the verse in Surah al-A'raf. The first difference: ﴿wa-idha qulna﴾ versus ﴿wa-idha qila﴾, and the Truth willed this in order to bring us a different image, as we have explained before. In the verse of al-Baqarah He (exalted is He) says ﴿Enter﴾, while in the verse of al-A'raf He says ﴿Dwell﴾. We know that entering is for an end, which is dwelling; that is, "enter so that you may dwell." He made this clear by saying in al-A'raf ﴿Dwell﴾, to show that their entry is not for passing through but for residence. And God willed to give them the ultimate end, since no one dwells in a town unless he has entered it.

Thus we see that the words of the Qur'an do not come for repetition, but for establishing and for bringing a new meaning that clarifies, explains and elucidates. The Truth says here in al-A'raf: ﴿and eat from it wherever you wish﴾. In the verse of al-Baqarah He says: ﴿so eat from it wherever you wish, in abundance﴾.

When God commanded them to enter and they were hungry, the Truth commanded them to eat immediately and at once, with expansiveness; therefore He brought the word "raghadan" (in abundance), because their need for food was intense and pressing. But after commanding them to dwell, He made clear to them that they should eat, because dwelling achieves stability and allows a person to eat with ease and deliberation. The Truth says here in al-A'raf: ﴿and say: "Remission," and enter the gate prostrating﴾. That is, He placed their saying "hittah" before the prostration, whereas in the verse of al-Baqarah He placed the prostration first, saying: ﴿and enter the gate prostrating and say "Hittah"﴾ (part of 2:58).

The Truth brought this difference because He knew that the emotional responses of the listeners differ at the moment of entry: there is one who is moved by the word, so upon entering he says what he was commanded, asking for remission and forgiveness of sin from God; and there is another who is moved by the deed, so he prostrates immediately upon entering, in compliance with God's command. Also the Truth said here in al-A'raf:

﴿We shall forgive you your sins, and We shall increase the good-doers﴾ (part of 7:161).

And in Surah al-Baqarah He says: ﴿We shall forgive you your transgressions, and We shall increase the good-doers﴾.

We know that the plural forms differ: there is the "broken plural" (jam' taksir) and the sound feminine plural (jam' ta'nith). In the broken plural we change the order of the letters of the word, as in our saying qufl (lock), whose plural is aqfal (locks). As for the sound feminine plural, we add an alif and a taa' to the word after removing whatever feminine marker the singular may have, as in our saying Fatimah, and Fatimat, and akla (a single meal), and aklat (meals). This is the sound feminine plural, meaning that the order of its letters does not change. The sound feminine plural indicates paucity, while the broken plural indicates abundance, reflecting the difference in degrees and proportions of sins; for the addressees are not equal in their sins: there are those who committed many errors and those who erred little. The difference also occurred at the end of the two verses: in al-Baqarah He said: ﴿and We shall increase the good-doers﴾.

The ending of al-A'raf came without the "waw" (and), saying: ﴿We shall increase the good-doers﴾.

The Truth has accustomed us and called us to say: "Forgive us, and You are the best of forgivers; have mercy upon us, and You are the best of the merciful; and write for us a good in this world." Here He (exalted is He) makes clear: I will not suffice with forgiving you and lifting your sins from you; rather I will increase you in goodness, and in this there is removal of harm and bringing of benefit. It is as if God, when He said "khatayakum" with the broken plural, which signals and indicates the abundance of sins and transgressions, and "khatiyatikum" which indicates paucity, they were preoccupied and asked: "And what after forgiveness, O Lord?" It was said to them: ﴿We shall increase the good-doers﴾. Will He forgive us only, or will He also reward us with good deeds? God's answer was that He would forgive them, increase them, and supply them with good deeds. We have drawn this detailed comparison between the verse of al-Baqarah and the verse of al-A'raf so that we know the verses do not contradict one another, but complete each other, in confirmation of the Truth's saying: ﴿And if it had been from other than God, they would have found in it much discrepancy﴾ (4:82).

Almighty God says next:

﴿So those who did wrong among them changed the word from what had been said to them, so We sent upon them a plague from the sky because they had been wrongdoing.﴾ (7:162)

This verse indicates that they split into two groups. Since God, glorified be He, said ﴿among them﴾, this means that some of them said and did what was required, while others did wrong and changed the saying. God had commanded them to say "ḥiṭṭa" (lit. "remove [our sins]") and asked them to enter the gate prostrating. The change on their part came in the saying, because speech may take place between a person and himself, such that no one else hears it. Action, however, is visible, which shows that some of them were showing off to others. In speech, they wanted to jest and say what is not fitting or proper, so instead of saying "ḥiṭṭa" they said "ḥinṭa" (wheat), mocking the word.

Thus we see that the substitution came in speech, while in action there was no speech involved. Some have said that the substitution also occurred in action on the part of some of them: instead of entering prostrating, they entered crawling on their buttocks, as a form of arrogance. But God did not mention anything of that, because their conduct in action may have been due to the fact that some of them were unable to act.

﴿So those who did wrong among them changed the word from what had been said to them﴾ (part of 7:162).

It is as if God is reminding them of how He cared for them during the wandering, how He shaded them with clouds, sent down manna and quails, and when Moses asked water for them, water came forth. But the instinct of substitution and rebellion did not leave them. Since they had altered the words of God, they must receive punishment: ﴿so We sent upon them a plague from the sky﴾.

There is a second verse in Surat al-Baqara in which God says: ﴿So We sent down upon those who did wrong a plague from the sky﴾ (2:59). The difference between "inzāl" (sending down) and "irsāl" (sending) is that inzāl happens once, whereas irsāl is continuous and sustained. For this reason God says of rain: ﴿And We sent down from the sky pure water﴾ (25:48), because rain does not fall from the sky all the time. But irsāl implies continuity, except for some of the effect of the air. That is why God says: ﴿And We send the winds fertilizing﴾ (15:22). Whatever requires continuity in the action, God describes with "arsala" (sent). As evidence, when God wanted to bring the flood to drown those who denied Moses, He said: ﴿So We sent upon them the flood﴾ (7:133).

When He wanted to encourage ʿĀd, the people of our master Hūd, to seek forgiveness, repent and turn back from the disbelief and sins they were in, He said to them:

﴿And O my people, seek forgiveness of your Lord, then repent to Him; He will send the sky upon you in abundant showers﴾ (11:52).

So irsāl means continuity, while inzāl is for a single time. God, glorified be He, wanted to bring us two snapshots from the story of the Children of Israel: He used the word "anzalnā" in one, and in another He used "arsalnā", because punishment varies according to the sinners, and sinners are graded by degree. One sin is small, another's sin is greater, and each person receives punishment according to the measure of his sin. Whoever commits a small sin, God sends down on him a punishment proportionate to it; and whoever persists, God sends upon him a punishment that continues in proportion to his great sins.

Here God says: ﴿So We sent upon them a plague from the sky because they had been wrongdoing﴾ (part of 7:162).

"Rijzan" means punishment. There is "rijz" and "rujz," and "al-rijz" arises from "al-rujz"; as in God's words: ﴿and the rujz, abandon it﴾ (74:5). That is, abandon the rujz, i.e., sins, transgressions and wrongdoings, so that you may be safe from the rijz, i.e., punishment. Here God shows that they received punishment because of their wrongdoing, while in the other verse He said: ﴿because they had been defiantly disobedient﴾ (2:59).

Defiant disobedience (fisq) precedes wrongdoing (ẓulm), because a person cannot wrong himself by violating the method unless he first becomes defiantly disobedient. For this reason God mentions the cause and then the effect. Thus we are assured that every word in the Qur'an comes for a fundamental meaning it conveys, and there is no repetition except for the whole story in itself. As for the snapshots of the story here and the snapshots of the story there, these are matters that come as foundations in each case to give meanings and fresh snapshots.

And the Exalted says after that:

﴿Ask them about the town that was by the sea, when they transgressed in the matter of the Sabbath, when their fish came to them openly on their Sabbath day, and did not come to them on the day they did not observe the Sabbath. Thus did We test them, because they used to defy (Our command).﴾

Here is a question about the town that was by the sea. We know that the first town they entered was Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis), and it was not on the sea. The town that was on the sea was Ayla, or Madyan, or Tiberias. The point is that it was "present by the sea" (hadirat al-bahr), meaning near the sea and overlooking it, because we say "fulan hadar," meaning he was far away and then drew near. Thus something like Alexandria could be called hadirat al-bahr.

As for His saying "wasalhum" ("and ask them"), the question here is directed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so that he would direct the question to the People of the Book, and ask them to look into their books in order to know that what he says is revelation from Allah to him. For they know that he (ﷺ) did not sit with a teacher, nor did he read in a book, and that what taught him was the One who sent him. He (ﷺ) does not wish to learn from them; rather he wishes to make them know that he knows. And they know that he has no source for his knowledge like the knowledge of the rest of mankind: he did not sit with a teacher, nor did he read in a book. You find in the Qur'an the phrase "ma kunta" (you were not), namely His saying, the Truth: "ma kunta" and "ma kunta" and "ma kunta" and "ma kunta," like His saying:

﴿And you were not on the western side when We conveyed to Musa the command﴾ (part of verse 44, Surah al-Qasas).

And like His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿Nor were you a dweller among the people of Madyan, reciting to them Our verses﴾ (part of verse 45, Surah al-Qasas).

And like His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿And you were not with them when they cast their pens, (to see) which of them would be the guardian of Maryam, nor were you with them when they disputed﴾ (part of verse 44, Surah Al 'Imran).

So, O Messenger of Allah, you were not with them to tell them what happened to them; rather that is present in their books. Therefore the One who taught you is the One who sent you. Likewise here, in confirmation of His saying:

﴿And you did not recite before it any Book, nor did you write one with your right hand; for then the falsifiers would have had cause for doubt﴾ (Surah al-'Ankabut, 48).

In this statement is a command from Allah, Glorified and Exalted, that He inform them that He has taught him and made him know what they cannot deny, so that they may be certain that Allah teaches him, and so that they may believe in Him.

﴿And ask them about the town that was by the sea﴾ (part of verse 163, Surah al-A'raf).

The word "wasalhum" resolves many difficulties. For example, the hadith of the Isra' (night journey), and that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) led the prophets in prayer with the prayer of Ibrahim.

On the authority of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I saw myself in al-Hijr, and Quraysh were asking me about my night journey. They asked me about things concerning Bayt al-Maqdis which I had not memorized, and I was greatly distressed, more than I had ever been distressed. So Allah raised it (Bayt al-Maqdis) up before me, and I looked at it. They asked me about nothing except that I informed them of it. I saw myself in a company of the prophets: Musa was standing praying, and he was a man with curly hair, as if he were one of the men of Shanu'ah. Isa was standing praying, and the one closest to him in resemblance is 'Urwah ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi. Ibrahim was standing praying, and the one closest to him in resemblance is your companion, meaning himself. Then the prayer time came, and I led them in prayer. When I finished, a speaker said: 'O Muhammad, this is Malik, the keeper of Hell,' so I turned to him, and he greeted me first with peace."(1)

And there is a verse in the Qur'an that says:

﴿And ask those of Our messengers whom We sent before you﴾ (part of verse 45, Surah al-Zukhruf).

The command to the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) is to ask the messengers of Allah who came before him. And when does he ask them? There must be an opportunity for them to meet, and then he asks. So when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) says that he met the prophets, spoke with them, and led them in prayer, the report is confirmed, because he has carried out Allah's command: ﴿And ask them about the town that was by the sea﴾. The question here is a question of confirmation, rebuke and reproach: "And what is the story of the town that was by the sea?"

We have said that "hadirat al-bahr" means near the sea, and we understand that what the verse addresses in asking them indicates that the sea has a role in it, because the matter concerns fish and catching. Therefore it must have been a coastal town.

﴿When they transgressed in the Sabbath, when their fish came to them openly on their Sabbath day, and on the day they did not observe the Sabbath they did not come to them; thus did We test them, because they used to defy (Our command)﴾ (part of verse 163, Surah al-A'raf). "Hitan" is the plural of "hut" (fish), just as they pluralize "nun," which also means fish, as "nunan"; it is a kind of fish. Allah forbade them to work on a specific day so that they would devote themselves to worship on it, and that day is "the Sabbath." Some of these customs still remain among them. One of them visited America and refused to ride a car on Saturday because it was a day of rest, and he likewise refused to work until the next day came. Allah, Glorified be He, willed to discipline them when they committed acts that contravened the method, and He took from them time for work, and said:

﴿For the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We forbade them good things which had been made lawful for them﴾ (part of verse 160, Surah al-Nisa').

In this there are examples and lessons for every deviant. To every deviant we say: beware of thinking that by deviating from the method of Allah you will take things from behind our Lord and steal them. No; for our Lord is able to afflict him with a punishment that exceeds what he took, thousands of times over. The one who accepts bribes, for example, Allah opens for him doors of diseases, ailments and calamities, so that everything he took is lost to him.

Thus the Children of Israel made lawful things that were forbidden, so Allah afflicted them by depriving them of things that had been lawful for them. Thus we see that the punishment that befell them was for their wrongdoing against themselves, because they were preoccupied with the worldly life and with material things; so work was forbidden to them on Saturday. Those who lived near the town by the sea were afflicted by Allah with a great trial: they would see fish in the water raising their fins like the sails of a ship, and the sails of the fish would appear to them while they were in their houses. This was a trial and a punishment from their Lord, because they were forbidden to hunt it, and they would see this fish before them on Saturday. But on the other days when work is permitted, such as Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday, not even a single fish would appear to them: ﴿And on the day they did not observe the Sabbath, they did not come to them; thus did We test them, because they used to defy (Our command)﴾.

Here they said: since our Lord has forbidden us to fish on Saturday, we must resort to a trick. They made a bag of braided wire, which we call "al-jawbiyyah," and they were the first to make this particular jawbiyyah. The fish would enter it and be unable to get out, so the fish would come on Saturday, enter the jawbiyyah, and they would extract it on Sunday. In this there is transgression. Or they would make a pool with an entrance but no exit, and in this there is deceit. And the heaven plotted against them with a stronger trick. Allah willed to test them because they defied the method and departed from obedience, and made lawful things that Allah had forbidden; therefore He forbids them things He has made lawful for others.

(1) Narrated by Muslim in his Sahih.

And when God says, after that: "And when a community among them said, 'Why do you admonish a people whom God is going to destroy or punish with a severe punishment?' They said, 'As an excuse to your Lord, and perhaps they will become righteous.'" (7:164)

Whenever you find that a group said something, there must be people to whom this statement was addressed. So in this situation there are "preachers" (qawm wa'izun), "those being admonished" (qawm mawa'uzun), and "a people who reject the admonition of the preachers" (qawm mustankirun wa'z al-wa'izin). Thus they became three groups:

Those who said the admonition to them, "Why do you not adhere to God's method?" These are the truly faithful believers. They said this because they saw those who opposed God's method. And those who blamed the preachers were the righteous people of the town who had despaired of the situation of those who opposed the method.

When we examine the verse: "And when a community among them said, 'Why do you admonish a people whom God is going to destroy'" (part of verse 164 of Surat al-A'raf),

we know that the speakers were of those who had not transgressed, and did not admonish, and they said this question to those who were being admonished, because they saw that admonition with those who depart from God's method is of no benefit. Just as God said to His Messenger (ﷺ): "Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they do not become believers."

Here God asks His Messenger: why do you grieve yourself and work to destroy your soul? Here some of the Children of Israel said: "Why do you admonish these people who exaggerate in disbelief? Why do you wear yourselves out with them? They are working toward God punishing them." And what did the preachers say? "They said, 'As an excuse to your Lord, and perhaps they will become righteous.'"

What is the "excuse" (ma'dhira) before God? It is said: "So-and-so made an excuse (a'dhara) to you" when you have done an act that outwardly appeared to be a fault, and then you clarify the reason for your action, as when you say to a friend: "You made me wait for you a long time, and you were late for our appointment." You say this to your friend because he has done a contrary act, namely being late for an appointment that he set with you. He replies: "My car broke down and I could not find transportation," and this is an excuse. So the meaning of "excuse" ('udhr) is to show a reason for a matter that contradicted the wish of another. That is why it is said: "He who warns has made an excuse (a'dhara man andhar)," and God says: "And those of the Bedouins who made excuses came" (9:90).

We also know that there is a mu'dhir and a mu'adhdhir. The mu'adhdhir is one who brings a false excuse, and the mu'dhir is one who brings a true excuse. The preachers said: "We admonish them, and you have judged that admonition is of no benefit with them, because they chose that God destroy and punish them. But we have not despaired, and even supposing we have despaired of their conduct, at least we will have presented to our Lord an excuse that we worked according to our capacity."

The word "wa'z" (admonition) requires us to say that there is a difference between conveying a ruling (balagh al-hukm) and admonishing with a ruling (al-wa'z bi'l-hukm). Admonition is to repeat to one being admonished what he knows but does not do. As when you say to a person: "Stand up for prayer," while he knows that prayer is required but does not perform it.

So admonition means reminding the heedless one of a ruling, and from the word wa'z comes the wu'azz (preachers). They are those who tell people the rulings that they know, so that they act upon them. Thus the preachers do not bring a new ruling.

Some scholars said: God's words, "Why do you admonish a people whom God is going to destroy," do not intend the group that did not commit the sin and did not admonish; rather, they intend the group being admonished, as if the ones being admonished said: "Our Lord will punish us, so why do you admonish us?" We say: No, because the end of the verse contradicts this. God says: "As an excuse to your Lord, and perhaps they will become righteous." The coming of "perhaps they" (la'allahum) confirms that this is a report about others, not that it is from those being admonished.

Then the Truth (al-Haqq) says: ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We saved those who forbade evil, and We seized those who did wrong with a grievous punishment, because they used to defy (the command of God).﴾

Here the Truth tells us that when those who were admonished forgot what some of the believers had admonished them with, God destroyed them with severe punishment, as a requital for their departure from the method and their defiance against it; and God saved the group that admonished. As for the third group, the one that did not join either the admonishers or the admonished, those who said: ﴿Why do you admonish a people whom God is going to destroy?﴾ — their saying is itself a form of admonition, for when they warn them that our Lord will destroy or punish whoever goes out against His method, this is admonition from another side.

And His saying, the Truth: ﴿When they forgot what they had been reminded of﴾ shows that others had admonished them and reminded them. The Truth punishes those who cast His method behind their backs and did not listen to those who admonished them, and departed from His teachings, so they wronged themselves and deserved the severe punishment. So the matter is not a case of God being arbitrary, because they were the cause of this, either through defiance (fisq) or through wronging themselves.

Then the Truth says, after that: ﴿So when they became arrogant about what they had been forbidden, We said to them: "Be apes, despised and rejected."﴾

Their being seized with a punishment shows that their lives were not taken away and that they were not made to die, because punishment is the infliction of pain upon one who feels pain, whereas death is not a punishment, since it ends the sensation of pain. Let us come to know the difference between death and punishment when we read the story of the hoopoe (hudhud) with Prophet Solomon. When Solomon noticed the hoopoe's absence, finding its place empty, he said: ﴿Why do I not see the hoopoe? Or is he among the absent? I will surely punish him with a severe punishment, or I will surely slaughter him﴾ (from verses 20 and 21 of Surat an-Naml).

Thus we see the difference between punishment and death. Here the Truth says: ﴿When they became arrogant about what they had been forbidden﴾. The word "'utuww" (ʿutuww, arrogance) means to refuse, to disobey, and to be haughty, so the punishment of God fell upon them, which the Truth made clear in His saying: ﴿Be apes, despised and rejected.﴾

For "ʿutuww" is pride and refusal, so God punished them by making them into the most base of animals; He made them like apes, each of them exposed in his shame, mocked and ridiculed by people. Did they then turn into apes? Yes. For when you command a person to do something, do you not first presume, before the command, that he is capable of doing it and of not doing it? And when God says: ﴿Be apes﴾, were they able to make themselves into apes? We say: this is called a "compelling command" (amr taskhiri), meaning: become and be transformed into apes. Those who admonished them saw them in this form, and this is here a statement of "report" (khabar) which we accept on the authentication of the one who said it, and this event was real for the one who witnessed it.

Therefore, as for the miracles that happened to our master the Messenger of God (ﷺ), other than the Qur'an, which has reached us as a book of guidance and a miracle and will remain so until the Hour arrives, did water not gush from between his fingers (ﷺ)? That and other miracles did happen, and his companions (ﷺ) witnessed them and told us the report, and it was a sign that confirmed their certainty and faith. It establishes for us a report: if your mind can accommodate it, then welcome; and if it cannot, do not let it stop your faith, because it is a sign that did not come for your sake. Every cosmic miracle that happened to the Messenger of God is intended for the one who witnessed it, and it reaches you as a report: if you trust the report, accept it; if you do not trust it and stop at it, your faith will not be diminished. Nevertheless, whoever receives the report through a certain (definitive) channel must accept it and submit.

Here the Truth has informed, by His saying ﴿Be apes, despised and rejected﴾, that He inflicted upon them a punishment by making them apes, despised and rejected; this is a punishment for those who were arrogant about what they had been forbidden. Those who admonished them, or who lived alongside them, are the ones who witnessed the punishment taking place.

As for whether a transformed person remains transformed: a person transformed into an ape or a pig remains in that state for a period so that whoever sees him, regarding him as wronged, will see him; then after that he dies and comes to an end.

Wa-idh ta'adhdhana Rabbuka la-yab'athanna 'alayhim ila yawm al-qiyamah man yasumuhum su' al-'adhab inna Rabbaka la-sari' al-'iqab wa-innahu la-ghafur rahim (7:167).

Then the Truth says: ﴿And when your Lord declared that He would surely send against them, until the Day of Resurrection, those who would afflict them with a terrible punishment. Indeed your Lord is swift in punishment, and indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ (7:167).

Ta'adhdhana (declared, proclaimed): its root is the hamzah, the dhal and the nun, from which comes udhun (ear), and adhan (call to prayer). All of them mean announcement (i'lam), and the means of announcement is the ear and hearing. Even the one whom we teach by writing, we tell him: "Listen." Then he writes and reads, and he reads only after he has heard, because he will not know reading except after he hears the names of the letters, "alif," "ba'," etc., and then spells them. So no one reads except after he hears, and thus hearing is the origin of knowledge. In the Qur'an we read: ﴿When the sky splits asunder (1), and hears and obeys its Lord, as it must (2)﴾ (Surah al-Inshiqaq).

"And hears its Lord" means it listened to its Lord; the moment He said to it, "Split," it complied and split.

﴿And when your Lord declared that He would surely send against them...﴾ (7:167): The discussion here concerns the Children of Israel. He, glory be to Him, makes clear that although they are free to act, "their faithful stances will remain fluctuating and wavering, and they will never cease spreading and propagating corruption. For this reason God will impose upon them one who will afflict them with a terrible punishment." And why?

Because they are attributed to a religion. God does not inflict punishment on the disbeliever in Him and the atheist, for by his disbelief and atheism he has left this circle, since God has not sent a messenger to him. But the one attributed to God in religion, the one attributed to God in message, the one attributed to God in a book: if he becomes corrupt while people know of him that he follows a prophet and that he has a book, then he becomes a bad example of corruption for people. So when God imposes punishment upon them, He imposes it not only because of corruption, but because it is corruption attributed to one who is attributed to God. We have learned that the root adhana is all centered on announcement, and when God spoke of our creation He said: ﴿And Allah brought you forth from the wombs of your mothers, knowing nothing, and He made for you hearing, sight and hearts﴾ (16:78).

The Truth, glory be to Him, calls the Arabs contemporary to the Messenger of God "unlettered" (ummiyyin), meaning they had none of the means of knowledge, and He, glory be to Him, created for us the means of knowledge, by giving us hearing, sight and hearts, which are the means of knowledge that begin with hearing, then sight, then the heart. It is remarkable that He arranged them in the performance of their function, because when a child is born, as we said before, if someone comes after his birth and places a finger before his eye, he does not blink, because his eye has not yet performed the function of sight. The eyes of a newborn do not perform the function of sight until after a period of three to ten days; but if you come to his ear and shout, he reacts.

This is evidence that his ear performed its function from the moment of birth, while his eye does not perform the function of sight until after a period. First comes hearing, then sight, and from hearing and sight information forms, and rational knowledge arises in a person. For example, they tell a child: "Beware of approaching this fire lest it burn you," and he does not believe it, and the sight of the fire attracts him so he touches it, and it stings him once. After the fire has stung him once, he no longer needs the statement to be repeated that fire burns. Rational knowledge has formed in him. So first hearing comes, then sight, then the hearts. For this reason He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿that you may give thanks﴾ (16:78), giving thanks to Him, glory be to Him, for providing you with the means of knowledge to bring you out of your unlettered state.

There is another miraculous point: when the Truth spoke of the means of knowledge, He mentioned hearing in the singular and sight in the plural, although both are instruments. He said "the hearing and the sights" and did not say "the hearing and the sight," nor "the hearings and the sights," because hearing is the instrument that picks up sounds, and by its nature it has no covering; but the eye is not so, for in its natural constitution there is a lid to close it. If you emit a sound from your mouth, everyone hears it, and so the locus of hearing is one; but in whatever scene you may have a desire to see, you open your eyes, and if you have no desire to see, you close them.

Thus the sights are multiple in what they show, while hearing is one, and you have no choice whether to hear or not. As for sight, you have a choice whether to see or not. These are matters the Truth arranged for us in the Qur'an before the science of physiology arose. He arranged them, glory be to Him, singling out hearing and pluralizing sight, although both serve one task. There is only one verse in the Qur'an: ﴿Indeed, the hearing, the sight and the heart, all of these will be questioned about﴾ (17:36).

The Truth said this because responsibility here is individual and personal, and each one is responsible for his own hearing, sight and heart, and is not responsible for the hearings, sights and hearts of others. We see that the root "hearing" has come first, and after it the root "sight" came, except in one verse also, which speaks of the Day of Resurrection: ﴿Our Lord, we have seen and we have heard﴾ (32:12).

Here the Truth placed the root of sight before the root of hearing, because on the terror of the Resurrection, when the hour comes, we will see a change in the universe before we hear anything.

﴿And when your Lord declared that He would surely send against them...﴾ (7:167). Ta'adhdhana means: God made a firm, emphatic announcement that you, Children of Israel, will remain in constant deviation, and therefore God will impose upon you one who will afflict you with a terrible punishment, either from a religious direction, as the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, did with Banu al-Nadir, Banu Qurayzah, Banu Qaynuqa' and Khaybar, or He will impose upon them a tyrannical ruler who is not religious, in confirmation of the Truth's words: ﴿And thus We make some of the wrongdoers allies of others﴾ (6:129).

Likewise what happened with Nebuchadnezzar and Hitler. So "and when your Lord declared" means your Lord announced with emphatic announcement, because humans may be informed of something, but their ability is not guaranteed to carry out what they have been informed of. If you inform someone of something, you may not possess the tools of execution; but God, glory be to Him, is the owner of the tools of execution, and His announcement is certain, so He announces a thing, whereas others, the surrounding circumstances may not help them to carry it out. An example: the early companions of the Messenger of God, being oppressed, could not protect themselves from the persecution of the polytheists and disbelievers, and each one sought a place where he could be safe; some went to Abyssinia, others went to a powerful one to seek protection. In these grievous circumstances God sent down a Qur'anic verse to the Messenger of God saying: ﴿The multitude will be routed and will turn their backs﴾ (54:45).

Some wondered how they could be routed when we are unable to protect ourselves. When this verse was revealed, our master Umar said: "Which host will be routed?" Umar said: When the day of Badr came, I saw the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, leaping in his armor, saying: ﴿The multitude will be routed and will turn their backs﴾, and then I understood its interpretation that day. God, glory be to Him and exalted, is the most knowing of victory, and He is able to carry out what He has announced according to what He announced, because there is no other god who opposes Him. So "and when your Lord declared" means He announced with emphatic announcement, and the basis of emphatic announcement is that no other power can prevent His ability or annul His judgment.

﴿And when your Lord declared that He would surely send against them until the Day of Resurrection﴾ (7:167).

That is, God will send against them one who will afflict them with a terrible punishment. In the text of the Qur'an there is one sent, and God leaves him free to deal with them, and God does not prevent them from him; rather God imposes punishment upon them by the choice of the wrongdoer. As the Truth said: ﴿Have you not seen that We sent the devils upon the disbelievers, inciting them with incitement?﴾ (19:83). That is, He sent them for this task and left them free to deal with those who listen to them: ﴿And when your Lord declared that He would surely send against them until the Day of Resurrection﴾.

The phrase "until the Day of Resurrection" indicates that this element, the troublesome Jews, will remain in existence like a leaven of disturbance until the Hour comes. Why?

They carry out the task of evil in existence. Were it not for the presence of evil in existence, and people being bitten by its harms and corruptions, none of the people would have rushed toward truth and goodness. So evil came to bite people with its pains and corruption, so that people would turn toward goodness. For this reason you find the strongest emotions stirring in the hearts of Muslims, and the strongest impulse toward Islam, when they see someone persecuting the cause of Islam.

The task of evil in existence is that it gathers the elements of good in existence, and the task of falsehood in existence is that it stirs the elements of truth and urges them to fight evil and oppose it; for when falsehood becomes widespread and people are distressed by it, they raise their hands and say: "O people, do good." If that did not happen, you would not find anyone turning to goodness with zeal and fervor.

﴿And when your Lord declared that He would surely send against them until the Day of Resurrection one who would afflict them with a terrible punishment﴾ (7:167):

And "yasumu" comes from the root sawama, which we hear in livestock, and we call them "sa'imah" (grazing), those that seek the means of their sustenance, and it is not their owner who prepares the means of their sustenance for them. As for animals that are tied up and are not grazing, they are those for whom someone prepares their food. So the origin of "sama" is to seek; a grazing beast is one that seeks its sustenance and food by itself.

"Sama" also means to seek punishment, and no one seeks punishment unless he has exhausted his strength in torment. He seeks from one who is able to torment that he torment, meaning God causes to go and sends against them one who carries out their torment with all his strength, and if his strength wanes or weakens, he seeks help in tormenting them from another.

So the seeking of punishment means: he himself tormented, and he was not content to have tormented, but sought for them another punishment; and "yasumuhum su' al-'adhab" means the evil, severe punishment. The Truth concludes the verse with His words: ﴿Indeed your Lord is swift in punishment, and indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ (7:167).

The meaning of the swiftness of a thing is that it takes less time than expected, for swiftness is the shortening of time. "Indeed He is swift in punishment" applies to this world and the Hereafter: the moment they commit a sin, He sends against them one who punishes them in this world; as for the Hereafter, there is great swiftness in it, because the distance of each person to punishment is not the lifespan of the world, for a person, as soon as he dies, the world ends for him. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "When one of you dies, his resurrection has come." (1)

There is swiftness in the reckoning of the Hereafter. And even if we suppose that we will all remain without reckoning until the world ends, the reckoning will still be swift, because every moment that passes over any person brings him closer to punishment; and even if the age of the world were a million years, every day that passes will decrease the age of the world.

And when the Truth, glory be to Him, says after the swiftness of punishment "And indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful," someone may ask: how, when the discussion here is about punishment? We say: it is He, glory be to Him, who speaks, and He is capable, so if He says "indeed He is swift in punishment," this means He hastens to punish the corrupt and the wrongdoers, because He is Forgiving, Merciful...

(1) Narrated by al-Daylami from Anas, traced to the Prophet.

Al-Sha'rawi, *Tafsir al-Sha'rawi* (surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66), on surah 7, verse 168:

After that, He, glorified is He, says: ﴿And We divided them into communities upon the earth; among them are the righteous, and among them are others than that; and We tested them with good things and bad things, that they might return.﴾ (7:168)

He, glorified is He, had also said before this: ﴿And We divided them into twelve tribes, as communities﴾ (part of 7:167).

But the statement here comes for a different meaning: ﴿And We divided them upon the earth into communities; among them are the righteous, and among them are others than that.﴾

The Truth (al-Haqq) has dispersed them so that they have no homeland, and they live in humiliation, because they have been in disagreement and not in agreement with one another from the beginning. They have been like this since they were tribes, sons, and brothers in constant discord. Here the Truth says: ﴿And We divided them upon the earth into communities﴾.

The meaning of "We divided them" is that each fragment has its own inner cohesion, and also that it does not spread out in the place where it lives. For this reason we said that they never dissolve into societies. As we have said, when you go to Spain you find for them a distinct quarter, and likewise in France, Germany, and every place where they have a separate gathering into which no one enters and from which they take no morals from anyone. The Truth willed this after He had said to them: ﴿Enter the holy land which Allah has written for you﴾ (5:21).

After He had bestowed upon them a land in which to settle, they said: ﴿Indeed, we will never enter it as long as they are in it. So go, you and your Lord, and fight. Indeed, we are sitting right here﴾ (5:24).

So Allah forbade them to settle in one homeland where they could gather, and He scattered them across the whole universe, because if they had been gathered together, their corruption would have been confined only to the circle in which they lived. Allah wills to proclaim to the whole world that their corruption is general corruption. For this reason, if they gather in one place, the forces will inevitably unite against them and either expel them or punish them. I think the recent events of Hitler are not far from memory. We have already clarified this in explaining His, the Truth's, saying: ﴿And We said after him to the Children of Israel: "Dwell in the land"﴾ (17:104).

We have said that "dwelling in the land" means that they are scattered throughout it, because He, glorified is He, did not appoint for them a specific place in which to live. So when the promise of the Hereafter comes, Allah will take vengeance upon them with a single blow, and the Truth will bring them together as a mass, as a crushing blow: ﴿And We divided them upon the earth into communities; among them are the righteous, and among them are others than that.﴾

There is a group of them who came to the illuminated city of Madinah, and the city accommodated them. They became people of knowledge, people of the Book, people of wealth and property, and people who built fortresses. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) migrated, he concluded a treaty with them. Whoever among them entered into faith deserved the treatment of believers: for them is what is for them, and upon them is what is upon them. The Truth has said:

﴿And among the people of Moses is a community who guide by the truth and by it act justly﴾ (7:159).

We have said that this is called the preservation of possibility for those who consider believing in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): ﴿And We divided them upon the earth into communities; among them are the righteous, and among them are others than that.﴾ And "others than that" (dūna) means "other than," so the counterpart of the righteous is the corrupt. Or it means: among them are the righteous at the summit, and among them are those who are less righteous. There are people who take the best, and people who take only the good. The Truth, glorified is He, continues: ﴿And We tested them with good things and bad things, that they might return﴾ (part of 7:168).

The phrase "that they might return" is what makes us understand that the saying of the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, "among them are righteous people, and among them are others than that," meaning disbelievers. For if they had done only the good and the better, the Truth would not have said ﴿that they might return﴾, or it would mean they return to the better.

"And We tested them" means We examined them, because Allah has absolute freedom in tests. He tests with blessing in order to know a reality about you, since He, glorified is He, knows it before you act. But His eternal knowledge is not considered testimony from us. Therefore He sets the test before us so that the result of our action becomes a testimony of acknowledgment against us: ﴿And We tested them with good things and bad things﴾. Glorified and exalted is He, He tests with blessing in order to see whether the servant is deceived by the means in this world rather than the highest Causer who bestowed them: ﴿No! Indeed, man transgresses, when he sees himself self-sufficient﴾ (96:6–7).

It is therefore obligatory that we thank the blessing and render it in the places of good for it. If the servant renders it with gratitude, he has succeeded; if he renders it otherwise, he fails the test. So there is a testing by blessings, and there is a testing by afflictions. The testing by afflictions is so that the Truth may see whether the servant is patient or not patient, that is, to see it and know it as an actual occurrence, for otherwise Allah had known it from eternity.

For this reason the Truth, glorified is He, says: ﴿As for man, when his Lord tests him and honors him and blesses him, he says, "My Lord has honored me." But as for when He tests him and restricts his provision, he says, "My Lord has humiliated me."﴾ (89:15–16).

We find someone who says, "My Lord has honored me," and someone who says, "My Lord has humiliated me," and the Truth clarifies: you are both liars. Blessing is not a proof of honor, and the withdrawal of blessing is not a proof of humiliation. Rather, honor arises when you receive blessing with gratitude and receive affliction with patience. So the coming of blessing in itself is only a test. Likewise, if Allah restricts your provision and narrows it for you, this is not for humiliation but for testing as well.

The Truth, may He be exalted, clarifies: ﴿No! Rather, you do not honor the orphan. And you do not urge one another to feed the poor. And you devour inheritance, consuming it greedily. And you love wealth with immense love﴾ (89:17–20).

You do not feed the orphan from your wealth, nor do you urge one another to feed the poor. How then can wealth be a blessing? It is a affliction upon you. Here the Truth says: ﴿And We tested them with good things and bad things, that they might return.﴾ And to Allah belongs the highest example: we say, "So-and-so has wearied me; I have turned him over on both sides. Neither severity benefited him, nor gentleness softened him, nor my generosity to him benefited him, nor my withholding benefited him." Allah tested the Children of Israel, and they did not return to obedience, which indicates that this is a disposition that has become rooted in them.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 7, verse 169:

Then the Truth (al-Haqq) says: ﴿Then there succeeded them a successor who inherited the Book, taking the goods of this lower life and saying, "It will be forgiven us." And if goods like it came to them, they would take it. Was not the covenant of the Book taken from them, that they should not say about Allah except the truth? And they studied what is in it. And the Last Abode is better for those who fear Allah. Will you not then use reason?﴾ (7:169).

Al-khalaf (successor), al-khalf, and al-khalifah are all the one who comes after another. It is said: "So-and-so is the khalifah (successor) of so-and-so." We have already read that Moses said to Aaron: ﴿Take my place among my people﴾ (7:142).

That is, be my khalifah. However, when you hear "khalf" with a sukun on the lam, know that it refers to corruption, and if you hear "khalaf" with a fatha on the lam, know that it refers to goodness. For this reason, when you pray for someone you say: "O Allah, make him the best successor (khalaf) to the best predecessor (salaf)." Here the Truth says: ﴿There succeeded them a successor (khalf)﴾. The discourse here is about them being the corrupt and the corrupters. The poet says:

"Gone are those among whose sides one used to live,
and left behind is a successor (khalf) like a mangy hide."

Here the poet laments the death of the generous and the openhanded. No one remains of those in whose spaciousness and generosity one used to live. Gone are those "among whose sides one lives," that is, in whose neighbourhood, because that neighbourhood was itself a blessing. When a man who is straitened and whose provision is restricted lives beside a good man who has blessing, the blessing of the good man overflows onto him. The poet here said:

"And left behind is a successor like a mangy hide," meaning that its skin is near and adhering, but it is the skin of a mangy camel.

We know the story of Abu Dulaf, a generous man in Baghdad. All people lived in his bounty, and whoever was in need he gave to. A contingency befell a poor neighbour of his, and he wanted to sell his house. He put the house up for sale, and they asked him about the price he would accept. He said: "My house is for a hundred dinars." But the neighbourliness of Abu Dulaf is worth a thousand dinars. This speech reached Abu Dulaf, and he said: "A man who values our neighbourliness at ten times what he values his house is truly worthy not to be wasted. Tell him: let him remain our neighbour and let him take whatever money he wants." ﴿There succeeded them a successor who inherited the Book.﴾ The Book is the Torah, and the successors took it as an inheritance, and a thing is not an inheritance unless the predecessor carries it faithfully and delivers it to the successor. But because they were people of corruption, let us see what they did with the Book. They inherited it. It was conveyed to them and they knew what was in it.

﴿They take the goods of this lower life and say, "It will be forgiven us"; and if goods like it came to them, they would take it.﴾ (Part of 7:169.) That is, they have no excuse for not being people of a better path. But they did not heed what is in the Book of the Torah of covenants, the lawful and the unlawful, "do this and do not do that"; they paid no attention to all of this, because they said to themselves: this Book gives distant bliss in the Hereafter, while they want near bliss. Among them were those who accepted bribery and exploited influence. Thus they took the goods (ʿaraḍ) of worldly life, which is the goods of the world. They did not take the management of the world by the method of Allah. The world contains essences (jawhar) and accidents (ʿaraḍ). The essence is the self-subsisting thing: a man, with his flesh and bone, is an essence; but his colour, whether dark or white, is an accident; short or tall, healthy or sick, rich or poor, these are accidents. So accidents are what come into being and pass away, while essences are what remain fixed for as long as their lasting has been decreed. As the logicians say: the essence is that which subsists by itself, and the accident is that which subsists by another.

They took the accident of the lower life, and the goods of the world may take the form of unlawful wealth, cheating, and considering bribery permissible. We know that a human being, even a believer, may commit a sin, and our Lord does not forbid this; for when the supreme Legislator prescribes a punishment for a crime, this indicates that it may occur. When the Truth says: ﴿As for the thief, male or female, cut off their hands﴾ (5:38).

The meaning of this statement is that a believer may be tempted by his soul to steal, for example, and the Truth has not left this crime without punishment. If we see a Muslim stealing, we say to him: this is an act that Islam forbids, and it has a punishment, and a criminal cannot commit a crime while adhering to the religion; rather he is merely attributed to the religion. When a Muslim commits a sin or disobedience and then repents, resolves that he will not return, his repentance is valid; and likewise if his sin persists and he returns to it and then repents. The important thing is that each time he does not persist in the act and then say: "I will repent later." But they persisted in disobedience and said: "Allah will forgive us." Indeed they did not even think of repentance, and we find among them one who says: ﴿We are the children of Allah and His beloved﴾ (5:18). The reply comes: ﴿Say: Why then does He punish you for your sins? Nay, you are human beings of those He has created﴾ (5:18).
